docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan
docs.t: 1.2.5 adds new features on top of 1.2.4 (which fixed what the first real-PC test found). Seven items, built and released in four stages so that each stage is tested on its own. Version: iso/VERSION 1.2.5, RVER 1.2.5.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan
docs.t: | # | Item | Size | Stage | |---|------|------|-------| | 7 | Blitzen: Lua, Luau and Pilot.lua | large | A | | 4 | Linux apps over Wi-Fi | small | A | | 5 | Games page in the App Store | small | A | | 3 | Windows in the Rudolf OS boot menu | medium | B | | 1 | Make a Rudolf OS USB stick | large | C | | 6 | Backup to a second USB stick | medium | C | | 2 | Hardware check in Task Manager | large | D |

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan
docs.t: Stage A is desktop and build work only (no new system programs); B touches the boot menu (Secure Boot tests); C and D add system programs and share the drive-writing code. One pull request per stage, each built to beta and tested in QEMU before the next starts; 1.2.5 goes to stable and gets a disc after stage D. ---

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 7. Blitzen: Lua, Luau and Pilot.lua
docs.t: > Stage A as built (branch rudolf-1.2.5-a). Differences from the plan below: > - Luau is built with clang 18 and the WASI libraries (as Emu's cores), not Emscripten: one lib/luau.wasm > (4.3 MB) holds the VM, the compiler and the type checker (Luau's Analysis library; there is no separate > luau-analyze.wasm). Luau's parser and checker use C++ exceptions, which wasi-sdk ships without, so > systools/mkluau.sh also builds LLVM 18's libcxxabi and libunwind for WebAssembly exceptions. > - Roblox scripts are checked against Roblox-lite (lib/roblox-lite.d.luau, lib/roblox-enum.d.luau, > written for Rudolf OS: the types Pilot.lua uses, with game, workspace and script left open) rather > than luau-lsp's full Roblox definitions (several MB). > - Pilot.lua's definitions are copied from the community LSP (MIT, lib/pilot.d.luau); the stand-in parts > (lib/pilot-parts.luau) print what they are asked to do. A Screen does not draw into a canvas and sensors > have no "parts" panel yet; a run is marked "simulated". > - Not done yet: the model-quality runs (15 prompts per language through the real model).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 7. Blitzen: Lua, Luau and Pilot.lua
docs.t: Blitzen's language list (BLZ_LANGS in desktop/blitzen26.js) is Auto, BlockLua, JavaScript, C++, Python. Lua is reachable only as BlockLua, whose reference card pushes the model toward one-statement-per-line block shapes. 1.2.5 adds three languages:

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 7. Blitzen: Lua, Luau and Pilot.lua
docs.t: | Language | What it is | Runs where | Checked by | |---|---|---|---| | Lua | standard Lua 5.3, any style | Fengari in the page (already shipped), offline, browser version too | running it | | Luau | Roblox's Lua dialect: type annotations, continue, +=, string interpolation, generalized iteration | the Luau VM compiled to WebAssembly, offline, browser version too | luau-analyze (types), then running it | | Pilot.lua | Luau microcontroller scripts for the Roblox game *Waste of Space* (parts, ports, screens, modems) | a simulator with stand-in parts (labelled "simulated"); the real thing runs only in the game | luau-analyze with the Pilot.lua type definitions, then the simulator |

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 7. Blitzen: Lua, Luau and Pilot.lua › Runtimes
docs.t: Lua: reuse blzRunLua (Fengari, 10 s limit, sys and gl libraries) without the BlockLua constraints. Luau: build Luau (luau-lang/luau, MIT licence) with Emscripten in CI, pinned to a release tag and checksum: lib/luau/luau.wasm + luau.js (the VM and compiler, about 1 MB) and luau-analyze.wasm (the type checker). blzRunLuau(code) runs in a Web Worker with the same 10 s limit and print capture as JavaScript; print, string, table, math, buffer, coroutine, utf8, os.clock/os.time are available; game, workspace, Instance and other Roblox engine objects are not, and Blitzen says so when code needs them.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 7. Blitzen: Lua, Luau and Pilot.lua › Runtimes
docs.t: Roblox scripts: code that uses Roblox engine APIs is type-checked against the Roblox definitions from luau-lsp (MIT licence, pinned file lib/luau/roblox.d.luau) and shown as "checked, not run" rather than failing.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 7. Blitzen: Lua, Luau and Pilot.lua › Runtimes
docs.t: Pilot.lua: lib/luau/pilot.d.luau, the API definitions (Part, Screen, Speaker, Modem, Disk, Keyboard, Microphone, sensors, StarMap, Gyro, Servo…), written for Rudolf OS from the public Pilot.lua documentation and checked against the community Luau LSP definitions (their licence decides whether we can copy or must rewrite). The simulator (blzPilotSim) provides those objects with logging stand-ins: a Screen draws into a small canvas in the answer, Speaker:Chat and Modem calls print what they would do, sensors return values set in a "parts" panel, GetPart/GetPartFromPort-style lookups return the stand-ins. Every simulated run is marked "Simulated: Waste of Space is not running".

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 7. Blitzen: Lua, Luau and Pilot.lua › Blitzen changes (blitzen26.js, blitzpacks26.js)
docs.t: BLZ_LANGS: Auto, BlockLua, Lua, Luau, Pilot.lua, JavaScript, C++, Python. blzLang: lua → Lua (BlockLua only when BlockLua is chosen), luau → Luau, pilot , pilotlua , pilot.lua → Pilot.lua; BLZ_LNAME` and the run/check list follow. blzRun: luau → blzRunLuau; pilot → analyze, then blzPilotSim.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 7. Blitzen: Lua, Luau and Pilot.lua › Blitzen changes (blitzen26.js, blitzpacks26.js)
docs.t: Context packs (each under about 800 words, like the others): - lua: Lua 5.3 language card plus Rudolf OS's sys and gl libraries, no block rules. - luau: the differences from Lua 5.3 (types, continue, compound assignment, interpolation, if expressions, generalized iteration, buffer), common Roblox patterns (Instance.new, services, events, RunService), and what runs here versus only in Roblox Studio. - pilot: Pilot.lua microcontroller basics (how a microcontroller gets its parts and ports, events, the most used part methods), and the rule "never invent part methods that are not in this card". BLZ_SYSTEM: lists the new languages and fences ( luau , pilot ).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 7. Blitzen: Lua, Luau and Pilot.lua › Blitzen changes (blitzen26.js, blitzpacks26.js)
docs.t: Fix-it loop: Luau type errors from luau-analyze go back to the model like runtime errors (up to 2 fixes). "Ask Blitzen" from the Code Editor: .LUA files ask Lua, a --!strict/--!nonstrict first line or .LUAU files ask Luau, a -- pilot first line asks Pilot.lua. The Code Editor gets .LUAU with Lua highlighting.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 7. Blitzen: Lua, Luau and Pilot.lua › Tests
docs.t: Host (iso/qt/shell2/blz_t.js, new): language list, fence detection, each runtime on a sample (Luau types, continue, interpolation; a Pilot.lua script that writes to a Screen and reads a sensor), the 10 s limit, a type error fed back to the fix loop (with a stand-in model reply). Model quality: 15 prompts per new language run through the real model in QEMU; record how many answers run or check clean on the first try and after fixes. A pack is rewritten if fewer than half pass. Browser version (the artifact): Lua and Luau run without rudolfd. ---

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 4. Linux apps over Wi-Fi
docs.t: rudolfd (api_apps install): drop the "needs a network cable" refusal; report the connection type and, for a download over 500 MB on Wi-Fi, the App Store asks first ("About 1 GB over Wi-Fi. Continue?"). Settings › Network › a network can be marked Metered: then every large download asks. Flatpak installs that stop are resumed (flatpak install again picks up the parts already fetched). Tests: QEMU with the virtual Wi-Fi (mac80211_hwsim) used by the Wi-Fi tests: install a small Flathub app over Wi-Fi; cut the link mid-download and resume.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 5. Games page in the App Store
docs.t: A Games tab in the App Store: Roblox (Sober), Steam (Flathub), Prism Launcher (Minecraft), RetroArch, and the built-in emulators and Quake, each with its size and a label Needs the graphics card or Runs anywhere. Uses 1.2.4's renderer check (Task Manager's "Drawn by"): when Rudolf OS draws with the processor, a note says which games will be slow and why, and links to Task Manager. Tests: host harness for the page and its labels; QEMU installs one game.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 3. Windows in the Rudolf OS boot menu
docs.t: > Stage B as built (branch rudolf-1.2.5-b). systemd-boot finds Windows only on the EFI partition it was started > from, and a Rudolf OS stick never has Windows there (Windows is on the computer's own drive). So Windows is > started through the firmware instead: Restart into Windows (Power dialog and Settings) sets BootNext to the > firmware's own Windows Boot Manager entry, once; Secure Boot checks it as the firmware always does. > auto-entries yes is set as planned, for a menu on a drive that also holds Windows. The test stand-in is unsigned, > so the Windows start is tested with Secure Boot off; with it on the firmware would refuse the stand-in.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 3. Windows in the Rudolf OS boot menu
docs.t: UEFI: at disc build time, iso/boot/sb/loader/loader.conf gets auto-entries yes, so systemd-boot lists Windows Boot Manager when it finds \EFI\Microsoft\Boot\bootmgfw.efi on any ESP, below the Rudolf OS entries. With Secure Boot on it is started by the firmware's own check (Microsoft-signed). BIOS: "Boot from hard disk" already exists in Rudolf Boot. Settings › Update and recovery › Boot menu: which entry starts by default and the wait (2–10 s), stored through systemd-boot's LoaderEntryDefault and LoaderConfigTimeout EFI variables (no file on the disc changes).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 3. Windows in the Rudolf OS boot menu
docs.t: Tests: QEMU (sb_t.py part G) with a second disk holding a stand-in "Windows" ESP whose bootmgfw.efi is a small EFI program signed by the Microsoft-keyed OVMF test key, with Secure Boot on and off; the default entry and timeout survive a restart.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 1. Make a Rudolf OS USB stick
docs.t: Settings › Storage and backup › Make a Rudolf OS USB stick… - Source: the running Rudolf OS (its image on the drive it started from) or a downloaded rudolf-os-*.iso in Downloads, checked as in "Install from" (rudolf-update verify-manifest). - Target: a removable drive of 2 GB or more that is not the running drive, picked from a list with model and size; an administrator confirms by typing the size shown. - Writes the image, reads it back and compares checksums, then adds RUDOLFDATA in the rest of the stick (the partition code of keepfiles.sh moves into /usr/lib/rudolf/partlib.sh, shared with install.sh). - Option: copy my files (this session's home folder) onto the new stick.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 1. Make a Rudolf OS USB stick
docs.t: mkstick.sh (new) does the work; rudolfd starts it as a job (POST mkstick?disk=…&image=…&files=0|1). Tests: QEMU with two virtual USB sticks: make a stick, then start from it with BIOS and with UEFI Secure Boot on (key enrolled); check files were copied when asked and not otherwise.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 6. Backup to a second USB stick
docs.t: Settings › Storage and backup › Back up everything › To a USB stick: writes the backup file (accounts' files still encrypted, settings, the apps list) onto a plugged-in drive as one file with a checksum file beside it. First start (no account yet): Restore from a backup finds backups on plugged-in drives. Tests: QEMU with a second virtual stick: back up, factory reset, restore; a damaged backup is refused.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 2. Hardware check in Task Manager
docs.t: > Stage D as built (branch rudolf-1.2.5-d): desktop/hwcheck30.js. Sound plays on the output in use (other > outputs are chosen in Settings › Sound and checked again); the download test is rudolf-update speedtest (the newest > release's kernel, about 10 MB, from the update server) through rudolfd's speedtest; sleep uses the real-time clock's > wake alarm (power?action=suspend&wake=10). The result is kept and is one line of the system report. Task Manager › Hardware › Check this computer…: a guided check of about a minute, one step per screen. Sound: a tone on each output (speakers, headphones, HDMI/DisplayPort): "Did you hear it?" Microphone: a 3-second level meter.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › 2. Hardware check in Task Manager
docs.t: Network: wired link speed (with the 1.2.4 cable hint), a Wi-Fi scan, a download test to the update server. USB: "plug in a USB stick" and watch it appear. Graphics: a WebGL scene with frames per second, the renderer and glamor state. Sleep (optional, laptops): suspend for 10 seconds and wake; check screen, network and sound come back. Result: a pass/fail list; "Report a problem" attaches it to the system report (no personal data). Tests: host harness for the flow; QEMU for sound (the virtual HDA card), USB and network. ---

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › Release steps (each stage)
docs.t: 1. Branch rudolf-1.2.5-<stage>, implement, host tests, local release build from the published beta. 2. Test disc (debug, test keys) and the stage's QEMU tests; existing suites must still pass: sb_t.py (31), t124_t.py (18), v120_t.py (34), tm_t.js, dl_t.js. 3. Pull request; after merge, build to beta and check the published files. 4. After stage D: CHANGELOG 1.2.5, promote to stable, disc disc-1.2.5 from disc-1.2.4.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › Risks
docs.t: Luau in WebAssembly: the Emscripten build must stay small and start fast; if luau-analyze is too large for the page, type checks run only on the installed system (a native luau-analyze in the base layer). Pilot.lua accuracy: the game changes its API; the definitions file carries its date and source, and Blitzen's answers say they are checked against that date's API. Licences: Luau and luau-lsp are MIT (fine to ship with their notices). Pilot.lua's community definitions need their licence checked first; without one, Rudolf OS writes its own definitions from the public documentation. Wi-Fi downloads of 1 GB on slow networks: resume and a clear size warning cover it.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.5 update plan › Risks
docs.t: Windows in the boot menu: a firmware that lists Windows twice (its own entry and ours) is harmless.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 1. "Check this disc" reports every disc as damaged
docs.t: What happens. At start-up, the menu entry *Check this disc or USB drive for errors* (UEFI: rudolf-check.conf, BIOS: item 3, both rudolf.check=1) runs sha256sum -c rudolf/sha256 in the initramfs. Every Rudolf OS disc and every stick written from one fails on boot/rboot.bin. The user sees "ERRORS FOUND - this disc or USB drive is damaged. Make a new one.", which isn't true. Making a new stick doesn't help, because the new one fails the same way.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 1. "Check this disc" reports every disc as damaged
docs.t: Why. systools/mkdisc.sh writes RUDOLF/SHA256 from the file tree. After that, mkimage.py writes the ISO and patches the kernel's place on the disc (RBTB + LBA + size) into the copy of BOOT/RBOOT.BIN on the image. So the file on the disc never matches its line in the list. This has been the case since 1.1. The published disc-1.2.4 and disc-1.2.5 both show it: every other file matches, and boot/rboot.bin fails. Fix. mkimage.py iso: after it patches the boot loader, it recomputes that file's SHA-256 and rewrites its line in RUDOLF/SHA256. The list file isn't in its own list, so the change is safe, and the list stays complete. An option, --sums RUDOLF/SHA256, names the list. mkdisc.sh passes it.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 1. "Check this disc" reports every disc as damaged
docs.t: initramfs init: discs already made (1.2.5 and older) must stop reporting damage too, once their computer has installed 1.2.6, because the updated kernel brings the new init. So the check compares boot/rboot.bin separately. The file is fine if the list's hash matches, or if the hash matches after the 8 bytes after RBTB are zeroed (the file as it was before patching). Every other file is checked as before. The check's report names the files that failed and says how many were checked, for example "1 312 files checked, all intact". At the moment it only prints the lines that aren't OK. Test. sb/t126a_t.py:

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 1. "Check this disc" reports every disc as damaged
docs.t: Start the test disc with rudolf.check=1. The debug entry gets a rudolf-check-debug twin, in test discs only. Expect "All files are intact" in /etc/rudolf/check.txt. Then flip one byte in a copy of the disc's DESKTOP.SFS and expect "ERRORS FOUND", naming rudolf/desktop.sfs. On the host, run a unit check of mkimage.py: the rewritten line matches the patched file on the image.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 2. Make a Rudolf OS USB stick refuses a stick that is already formatted
docs.t: What happens (from the code; to be confirmed first in QEMU with a FAT stick). When a USB stick is plugged in, devplug mounts its partitions under /media/sdX1, and so on. Sticks come formatted FAT32 or exFAT from the shop. *Make the stick…* goes from stick30.js to rudolfd mkstick to mkstick.sh to install.sh. install.sh stops at grep -q "^$DEV" /proc/mounts: "/dev/sdb is in use. Unmount its partitions first." The page doesn't unmount the stick first, and the page has no Unmount button for this. So on a real computer the feature only works with a blank or Rudolf OS stick. Rudolf OS doesn't mount its own sticks, because devplug skips iso9660 and RUDOLFDATA.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 2. Make a Rudolf OS USB stick refuses a stick that is already formatted
docs.t: The stage C test used a blank 4 GB image, so it never met a mounted stick. Fix. mkstick.sh, before install.sh, does three things: - Marks the disk busy: /run/rudolf/busy/<sdX>, which devplug honours. While the file is there, devplug mounts nothing on that disk. Without this, the partitions that --rereadpt brings back, among them the image's EFI partition, would be mounted again. - Unmounts every partition of that disk that is mounted under /media/, and only there. Anything mounted elsewhere still counts as in use, as before. - Says which drive was unmounted. The busy mark is removed on exit, whether the script succeeds or fails, by a trap.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 2. Make a Rudolf OS USB stick refuses a stick that is already formatted
docs.t: If a program still has a file open on the stick, umount fails. The message then says to close what uses the drive (Files, a Linux app), not "Unmount its partitions". stkConfirm (the page) says that the drive's current files and name will be erased, and shows its label when it has one. The text already says "Everything on it is erased." *Install here* has the same check. Internal disks aren't auto-mounted, but an external USB disk is. The same unmount runs there, only for /media/ mounts. Test. t125c_t.py gets a second stick: 4 GB, FAT32, label SHOPSTICK, holding one file. Rudolf OS mounts it at start.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 2. Make a Rudolf OS USB stick refuses a stick that is already formatted
docs.t: *Make the stick* must succeed on it, and must leave nothing mounted from it during or after. The new stick then starts as in step 2 of that test. Separately: the same request while a shell holds a file open on the stick must give the new message, and the stick must stay unchanged.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 3. CHANGELOG 1.2.5: date and component versions
docs.t: The 1.2.5 entry says (2026-10-19). The release that went to stable was built on 2026-10-23. It becomes (2026-10-23). The entry also doesn't mention that the release carries Chromium 156.0.8078.47 and Linux 6.18.58. A scheduled rebuild picked these up before the promote; the stable channel's notes line says only "Chromium …". Add one line: "Updated: Chromium 156 and Linux 6.18.58 (security fixes)." The stable notes line itself is fine. devices26.js already shows the CHANGELOG summary when notes only names a component. 1.2.6's own entry is written in stage A and grows with each stage.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 4. Tests that would have caught 1 and 2
docs.t: Above: t126a_t.py covers the disc check, and the second stick goes into t125c_t.py (renamed t126c_t.py). Release steps: the regression suites (sb_t.py, t124_t.py, v120_t.py, tm_t.js, dl_t.js) run on the final beta, the one being promoted, and not only per stage. For 1.2.5 only the four stage tests were re-run on 2026102311. A scheduled rebuild can replace the beta between the tests and the promote; that happened with 1.2.5 (2026102102 → 2026102311). So the promote input is the tested serial, and the tests are re-run if the beta changed. This is a note in RELEASES.md, not a code change. ---

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 5. More USB Wi-Fi adapters (stage B)
docs.t: > As built (branch rudolf-1.2.7-b). Differences from the plan below: > - Firmware. wififw.py runs only in the full disc build, so a release build does not pick firmware up by > itself. A release build takes firmware from the pinned list in firmware-extra.txt (fwextra.py). The eight > files and three links are pinned there with their SHA-256: htc_9271.fw, htc_7010.fw, > ath9k_htc/htc_*-1.4.0.fw, mediatek/mt7601u.bin, mediatek/mt7610u.bin, mediatek/mt7662.bin and > mt7662_rom_patch.bin. They are added to the CI build's sparse linux-firmware checkout. > - Kernel options. MT76x0U and MT76x2U have lower case in their names, and scripts/config upper-cases > names unless given --keep-case. So kconfig.sh has an mk helper for them; with m they would have been > left out without a word. No other option in the file is affected. > - mt76x2u firmware names. The driver asks for mt7662.bin and mt7662_rom_patch.bin, not the mt7662u… > names in the table below.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 5. More USB Wi-Fi adapters (stage B)
docs.t: Now. Rudolf OS already drives most current USB Wi-Fi adapters: Realtek RTL8188/8192 (rtl8xxxu), RTL8811AU/8812AU, RTL8821CU, RTL8822BU/CU, RTL8852BU, RTL8851BU (rtw88, rtw89); MediaTek MT7921AU and MT7925U; Ralink RT2800 (rt2800usb). A plugged-in adapter appears in Settings › Network like a built-in card, and Devices lists it as a "Wi-Fi adapter". Missing (kconfig.sh line 48), so these adapters show as a plain USB device and Settings says "No Wi-Fi adapter was found":

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 5. More USB Wi-Fi adapters (stage B)
docs.t: | Driver | Chip | Typical adapters | Firmware (linux-firmware) | |--------|------|------------------|---------------------------| | ATH9K_HTC | Atheros AR9271, AR7010 | TP-Link TL-WN722N v1, many "Linux-friendly" 2.4 GHz adapters | htc_9271.fw, htc_7010.fw | | MT7601U | MediaTek MT7601U | low-cost 150 Mb/s nano adapters | mt7601u.bin | | MT76x0U | MediaTek MT7610U | AC600 dual-band adapters | mediatek/mt7610u.bin | | MT76x2U | MediaTek MT7612U | AC1200 adapters, among them Alfa AWUS036ACM | mediatek/mt7662u.bin, mt7662u_rom_patch.bin | Change. Add the four options to the m line in kconfig.sh. Each one depends on USB and MAC80211 (already there) and pulls in its common parts by itself (ATH9K_HW, ATH9K_COMMON, MT76x02_USB, and so on).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 5. More USB Wi-Fi adapters (stage B)
docs.t: The firmware needs nothing extra. Each driver declares its files with MODULE_FIRMWARE, and systools/wififw.py copies exactly those from linux-firmware into the modules layer. Licences come along with linux-firmware's WHENCE entries, as for the others. Expected cost: roughly 0.5 MB of modules and 0.3 MB of firmware. devplug already names these as "Wi-Fi adapter" (by their network interface), and wifi.sh uses the first wireless interface. With a built-in card and a dongle both present, wifi.sh still takes the first one; picking the adapter is a separate, later item. CHANGELOG: "New: more USB Wi-Fi adapters work (Atheros AR9271, MediaTek MT7601U, MT7610U, MT7612U)."

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 5. More USB Wi-Fi adapters (stage B)
docs.t: Test. QEMU has no USB Wi-Fi device, so the test checks the built release instead (t126b_t.py on the test disc's serial shell): each new module is in the modules layer and loads (modprobe; without hardware it loads and stays idle); modinfo lists the USB IDs for one known adapter per driver (for example usb:v0CF3p9271 for the AR9271); each declared firmware file is in /lib/firmware. The existing MAC80211_HWSIM Wi-Fi test still passes. If you have one of these adapters, a short check on a real PC (join a network, run the hardware check's network step) completes it.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 5. More USB Wi-Fi adapters (stage B)
docs.t: Risk. These drivers are mainline and long-standing. AR9271 and MT7612U are the usual recommendation for Linux, so the main risk is size, which is small.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 6. Faster first Luau type check (stage B)
docs.t: > As built. > - The compiled WebAssembly.Module was already shared, so "compile once" needed no change. > - The new parts: > - a checker per kind; > - a warm message; > - replies dispatched by id: the old code replaced the Worker's onmessage on each check, so two checks at once > could mix up their answers; > - an idle end after 10 minutes. > - Tests: > - luau_t.js 29/29, with a warm Pilot.lua check in 7 ms against a 1.1 s load on the host; > - blz_t.js 14/14 (Blitzen's picker, and Code Editor with a Roblox .LUAU file). Now (desktop/luau30.js). The type checker runs in one Web Worker (LUAU.checker), kept between checks.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 6. Faster first Luau type check (stage B)
docs.t: The first check of a kind loads luau.wasm (4.3 MB), then defines that kind's types: Roblox-lite and its Enum for roblox; those plus pilot.d.luau for pilot. The first check is allowed 120 s, later ones 20 s. Changing kind (a Pilot.lua check after a Roblox one, or back) loads and defines everything again, because the Worker holds one kind at a time (checkerKind). On a slow computer, the first Pilot.lua check in Blitzen or Code Editor takes up to two minutes, and the program says "(not type-checked: …)" if the time runs out. Change. One Worker per kind (LUAU.checkers[kind]), each kept once loaded. That costs about 30 MB of memory per kind in use. Switching kinds no longer starts over.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 6. Faster first Luau type check (stage B)
docs.t: Warm-up. The checker for a kind is started in the background, after the page is idle (requestIdleCallback, at most one at a time), when: - Blitzen opens with Luau or Pilot.lua chosen, or a pack for them is opened; - Code Editor opens a .LUAU file (Luau, or Pilot.lua when the file uses GetPart). It defines the types with an empty program, so the first real check only checks. Compile once. luauModule() keeps the compiled WebAssembly.Module and gives it to each Worker, so luau.wasm is compiled once per session, not once per kind.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 6. Faster first Luau type check (stage B)
docs.t: Waiting. While a warm-up is still running, a check waits for it (with the 120 s limit counted from the warm-up's start) rather than starting a second load. Test. shell2/luau_t.js gets three timings: a warm-up made at idle, then a Pilot.lua check (expected under 3 s on the host); a Roblox check after it; and a Pilot.lua check again, with no reload (the Worker's define count stays 1 per kind). luau_pw.js (Code Editor): opening a .LUAU file starts the warm-up.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 7. Copy folders from a USB drive or memory card (stage B)
docs.t: > As built. > - rudolfd already had fs/tree (every file below a folder, in one call), so no rudolfd change. > - The copy goes to Downloads, or to C: when there is no Downloads folder; the notice says which. > - Test: files_t.js 8/8. Now (desktop/files25.js, remoteImport). A plugged-in drive (USB stick, memory card, external disk, under /media) opens in Files as a remote place. *Copy into Downloads* takes single files only: a folder gives "Copy folders one file at a time for now." Each file has a 256 MB limit.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 7. Copy folders from a USB drive or memory card (stage B)
docs.t: Rudolf OS does not mount phones (devplug lists them as "Phone or camera"), so this item is about drives. The old "from a phone or another computer" wording was wrong. Change. A selected folder is walked through rudolfd's fs/list and copied with its subfolders into Downloads. The folder keeps its name, made unique as for files. Before copying, the walk counts the files and adds up their sizes. It stops early if the copy would not fit (navigator.storage.estimate(), leaving 10 % free) or holds more than 5 000 files, and says which.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 7. Copy folders from a USB drive or memory card (stage B)
docs.t: A progress line in the status bar shows "Copying 120 of 431 files (34 MB)…", with Cancel. A cancelled copy keeps what was copied so far and says so. File names follow the same rules as single files (upper case, \ : * ? " < > | replaced). Files over 256 MB are left out and listed at the end, as are files that cannot be read. One fsSave() at the end, not one per file. Test. shell2/files_t.js (new) uses the stand-in rudolfd with a drive holding a tree three folders deep, 40 files, one file over 256 MB and one unreadable file. It checks: the copy, with the folder layout, names and content;

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 7. Copy folders from a USB drive or memory card (stage B)
docs.t: the two files left out, and listed; Cancel halfway; the "does not fit" refusal, with a small storage estimate.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 8. Hardware check: more steps, and the webcam driver (stage C)
docs.t: Now (desktop/hwcheck30.js). Six steps: sound, microphone, network, USB, graphics, sleep. Two gaps: No webcam driver. The kernel has no UVC driver (kconfig.sh has no MEDIA_SUPPORT and no USB_VIDEO_CLASS), so no webcam works in Rudolf OS, built-in laptop cameras included. Devices lists one as "Camera" and nothing can use it. No battery health. rudolfd's battery reading (/sys/class/power_supply) gives only capacity, status and online. Change. Kernel. Add MEDIA_SUPPORT, MEDIA_USB_SUPPORT, MEDIA_CAMERA_SUPPORT, VIDEO_DEV and USB_VIDEO_CLASS as modules (uvcvideo needs no firmware), so Chromium's camera access (getUserMedia) works. Webcams then work in web pages and Linux apps too: a CHANGELOG line of its own.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 8. Hardware check: more steps, and the webcam driver (stage C)
docs.t: rudolfd. GET battery also reports energy_full and energy_full_design (or the charge_* pair on batteries that report charge), cycle_count when there is one, and the maker and model.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 8. Hardware check: more steps, and the webcam driver (stage C)
docs.t: Five new steps, after graphics and before sleep. Each can be skipped, and each result goes into the system report as the existing ones do: 1. Keyboard. A keyboard drawn on screen (the chosen layout from Settings › Keyboard). Each key lights when pressed; "Every key works" or "These did not answer: …" after the user says they are done. The function and Rudolf keys that rudolf-display takes for itself (Ctrl+W/T/N/Q) are shown as reserved, not as failures. 2. Touchpad or mouse. A box to draw in: the pointer trail, the left and right buttons, and scrolling with the wheel or two fingers. Each of the four lights when seen. 3. Camera. Lists the cameras (enumerateDevices) and shows the first one live, with a switch for the next. The result is "Camera works" if frames arrive, or "No camera was found". With no camera at all the step is skipped by itself. Nothing is recorded or saved. 4. Battery. Only on computers with a battery. Shows "Health: 87 % of its design capacity (52.1 of 60.0 Wh), 312 charge cycles", with a note below 70 % ("holds noticeably less than new"). Shows "Charging" or "On battery" from status. 5. Screen.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 8. Hardware check: more steps, and the webcam driver (stage C)
docs.t: Full screen, one colour at a time (black, white, red, green, blue), a tap or key for the next, to spot dead or stuck pixels. The user answers "Looks even" or "I saw spots". Test. shell2/hw_t.js (page, stand-in rudolfd): the five steps' results with stand-in key, pointer and battery readings. sb/t127c_t.py (QEMU, extending t125d_t.py): - QEMU's USB webcam (-device usb-video) as a UVC camera, giving frames through the new driver; - keyboard and tablet input sent through QMP; - a battery from QEMU's acpi test battery, if the build has one, or else the page test only.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 9. Make a stick or Install from the downloaded parts (stage B, moved from C)
docs.t: Now. disc-1.2.x comes as 18 parts (GitHub's file size limit). Before *Make a Rudolf OS USB stick* or *Install from* can use it, the user has to join the parts with the commands in JOIN-PARTS.TXT, and Rudolf OS has no way to do that from the desktop. rudolfd's install/images lists only whole .iso files in Downloads. Change. install/images also lists sets of parts: NAME.iso.part00 … partNN with no gaps, and NAME.iso.sha256 next to them. Each set shows as "rudolf-os-1.2.7.iso (18 parts, not joined)".

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 9. Make a stick or Install from the downloaded parts (stage B, moved from C)
docs.t: Choosing one runs a job, install/join: - check the free space (the image size plus 64 MB); - join the parts in order into Downloads/NAME.iso.joining; - compare its SHA-256 with the .sha256 file; - rename it to NAME.iso. The job log shows progress, and a damaged or missing part is named ("part 07 does not match: download it again") using the same checks as join.ps1. The image then goes on, as today, to the Make a stick or Install from step that was chosen. That step still checks the image's signed release list itself. After a successful join, the dialog offers to delete the parts (548 MB). Test. shell2/stick_t.js: the set is listed and offered; a missing part is reported.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 9. Make a stick or Install from the downloaded parts (stage B, moved from C)
docs.t: sb/t127c_t.py (QEMU): the real disc-1.2.6 parts (or a test disc split the same way) in Downloads are joined, checked, and a stick is made from the result, then started. A part with one byte changed is named, and nothing is written to the stick.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 9. Make a stick or Install from the downloaded parts (stage B, moved from C)
docs.t: > Changes to item 9 for the real laptop (found there): > - The .sha256 is not on the disk. Downloads of 1.5 MB or less stay only in the browser's storage > (C:\DOWNLOADS), and the 86-byte .sha256 is one of them. So the page reads the expected hash from it (from the > browser's storage or from the disk) and passes it to install/join. With no .sha256 at all, the join goes on. > The stick or installation still checks the image's signed release list; the dialog says the parts were joined > without a checksum. > - Part names. Large downloads are kept on the disk under the name the browser gave them (rudolf-os-1.2.6.iso.part00). > The page shows them in capitals. Names are matched without case. > - What to choose. Make a stick's "Rudolf OS to put on it" lists the set as "rudolf-os-1.2.6.iso (18 parts, not > joined yet)". Choosing it joins first, in the same job log, then makes the stick.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 10. Make a stick refuses an older Rudolf OS stick (1.2.6 regression; stage B)
docs.t: What happens (real laptop, 1.2.6): Make the stick… on "sda — SanDisk 3.2Gen1 — 61.5 GB (an older Rudolf OS stick)" stops at once with "/dev/sda is in use: a file on it is still open. Close File Explorer…". Nothing on the stick is open. Why. Item 2 (1.2.6) added devplug release DISK before writing. Its first line refuses any system_disk, which means any disk with an iso9660 or RUDOLFDATA partition. Every Rudolf OS stick is one. install.sh reads the refusal as "busy" and gives the open-file message. Before 1.2.6, such a stick was simply written, since devplug never mounts it. t126c_t.py used only a blank stick and a shop-formatted one. Fix.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 10. Make a stick refuses an older Rudolf OS stick (1.2.6 regression; stage B)
docs.t: devplug release drops the system_disk refusal. It only ever unmounts mounts under /media, which devplug made itself and never makes for a Rudolf OS disk. The drive Rudolf OS runs from is already refused before it, by install.sh and mkstick.sh (/etc/rudolf/media). install.sh tells "could not unmount" apart from "nothing to unmount": release exits 0 when there is nothing to do, and 1 only when an unmount fails. Test. t126c_t.py gets a third stick: an older Rudolf OS stick (the 1.2.5 test disc written to a 4 GB image, with its RUDOLFDATA). Make a stick must succeed on it. The tests on the blank and shop-formatted sticks stay.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 11. "This Rudolf OS" copies boot files that cannot start with Secure Boot (stage B)
docs.t: What happens. Make a stick's first choice, "This Rudolf OS 1.2.6", copies the disc image of the drive Rudolf OS started from, plus the installed updates. On the laptop, that image comes from a pre-1.2.2 disc: its EFI partition has only EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI, unsigned, with no shim and no EFI/rudolf/. Updates replace the system (kernel and layers) but never the boot files. So the new stick would carry the same boot files, and the firmware refuses them with Secure Boot on ("Secure Boot Violation"). The same goes for Install here from "this Rudolf OS". Fix. rudolfd info reports bootSecure: whether the start-up drive's EFI partition has EFI/rudolf/rudolf.cer and a signed EFI/BOOT/grubx64.efi (checked with the certificate in the base layer).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 11. "This Rudolf OS" copies boot files that cannot start with Secure Boot (stage B)
docs.t: When it is false, Make a stick and Install here say so under "This Rudolf OS": "This computer started from a disc made before Rudolf OS supported Secure Boot (1.2.2). A stick made from it will not start with Secure Boot on. Choose a downloaded image instead." The choice stays available. Settings › Security › Prepare Secure Boot says the same, instead of making a MOK request that nothing will act on (no shim on the drive). The laptop got such a request. Test. stick_t.js: bootSecure false gives the note and the Security wording; true gives neither. t127c_t.py (QEMU, item 9's test): on the 1.2.6 test disc, rudolfd reports bootSecure true.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 12. Downloads in one place (stage B)
docs.t: What happens. Oracle saves downloads to C:\DOWNLOADS (dl27.js, dlCDir). Files over 1.5 MB stay on the disk in /home/rudolf/Downloads, with a reference in that folder. Files' sidebar "Downloads", the Downloads page's "Open Downloads folder" and Files' import all use C:\USERS\<name>\DOWNLOADS (homePath('DOWNLOADS')). So everything downloaded seems to vanish. On the laptop, the 18 parts were found only by typing C:\DOWNLOADS. Fix. Downloads go to the signed-in account's own Downloads (homePath('DOWNLOADS')), the folder Files shows. With nobody signed in, they go to C:\DOWNLOADS, as now.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 12. Downloads in one place (stage B)
docs.t: Existing downloads. Anything already in C:\DOWNLOADS (the browser-storage files, and the references to files on the disk) is moved once, at the first sign-in after the update, into that account's Downloads, after a notice ("12 downloads were in C:\DOWNLOADS; they are now in your Downloads"). The files on the disk do not move. /home/rudolf/Downloads is still where large downloads live (the references point there), so the stick and install tools find them as before. "Open Downloads folder" opens the same folder. Test. dl_t.js (host): a download, small and large, appears in the account's Downloads, the folder the sidebar opens; an existing C:\DOWNLOADS with three items moves on first sign-in, and the references still open.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 13. Download protection and a Rudolf OS release's own files (stage B)
docs.t: What happens. typeGate blocks every file type outside RECOG unless an administrator ticks "Allow saving file types Rudolf OS does not recognize". So .part00–.part17 and .sha256 are refused. .ISO is in HIGHRISK, so a joined image could not be downloaded at all. On the laptop the setting had to be turned on, and it was first left unapplied, so the parts were blocked. Fix.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 13. Download protection and a Rudolf OS release's own files (stage B)
docs.t: A Rudolf OS release file is let through without changing that setting, when two things hold: - its name is rudolf-os-<version>.iso.partNN, rudolf-os-<version>.iso.sha256 or rudolf-os-<version>.iso; - it comes from this project's GitHub releases. The download record keeps the address the file came from, which on the laptop was https://release-assets.githubusercontent.com/github-production-release-asset/1414456577/…, and 1414456577 is this repository's id (gh api repos/merciless146/RudolfOS --jq .id). So the check is: that host (or objects.githubusercontent.com, GitHub's older one) and that id in the path. Nothing about them is trusted because of this. Make a stick and Install from still accept only images whose release list is signed with a key Rudolf OS trusts. The antivirus still scans them.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 13. Download protection and a Rudolf OS release's own files (stage B)
docs.t: Other .iso files stay blocked. The activity log says "allowed: a Rudolf OS disc image part from the Rudolf OS releases". Test. dl_t.js: the three names from the release address are kept; the same names from another site are blocked; random.iso from the release address is blocked.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 14. The Linux terminal does not start on an updated installation (stage B)
docs.t: What happens (laptop, 1.2.6, slot a, kernel 6.18.58, RUDOLFDATA 116 GB): Debian 13.7 is set up (149 MB), and Open Terminal says "rudolf-debian: the Debian sandbox did not start". rudolf-debian gives that one message for every failure inside the sandbox's start: _exit codes 2–4 and 10–18 cover unshare, the mounts, pivot_root and the ready signal. So the cause is unknown. The same 1.2.6 starts the terminal in QEMU, on a RUDOLFDATA made by a 1.2.x installer. Plan.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 14. The Linux terminal does not start on an updated installation (stage B)
docs.t: 1. Reproduce. In QEMU, install from disc-1.1.2 (or disc-1.2.0, whichever matches the laptop: its boot partition has only EFI/BOOT) onto a virtual NVMe disk with Install here. Then update through a stand-in stable channel to 1.2.6, as the laptop did, and set up Linux. The candidate causes, each checked there: - RUDOLFDATA made by the older installer: file system features (dumpe2fs; for example ext2/ext3 without extent/huge_file, a 128-byte inode size), and mount options; - folders the newer start-up expects under /persist and that only newer installers make; - /persist/debian left from an earlier setup, with other owners or modes.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 14. The Linux terminal does not start on an updated installation (stage B)
docs.t: 2. Report the cause (item 16): the sandbox start passes its _exit code and errno back to the starter, which prints "the Debian sandbox did not start: pivot_root failed (Invalid argument)". 3. Fix what step 1 finds. Most likely a repair at start-up (rudolf-init), so an existing installation is fixed by the update itself without erasing anything: making missing folders, correcting owners, or enabling a missing ext4 feature, if the cause is the file system. Erasing or reformatting is never done by itself. If only a reformat would fix it, Settings says so and offers Back up first. Test. t127d_t.py (QEMU): install from the old disc, update to 1.2.7, then Open Terminal runs echo ok in Debian;

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 14. The Linux terminal does not start on an updated installation (stage B)
docs.t: the same on a fresh 1.2.7 installation; with a forced failure (a test-only switch), the message names the failing step.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 15. Flatpak downloads fail with O_TMPFILE on the same installation (stage B)
docs.t: What happens. App Store › Linux apps › Download the app list, and Games › Roblox (Sober), both fail: "While pulling appstream2/x86_64 from remote flathub: open(O_TMPFILE): No such file or directory". Flatpak's repository is /var/lib/flatpak, a bind of /persist/flatpak (rudolf-init). O_TMPFILE gives ENOENT when the directory it is given is missing, or when the file system under it cannot make unnamed files. So this points at the same RUDOLFDATA as item 14, which is why the two are looked at together. Plan. The same reproduction as item 14: check /persist/flatpak/repo/tmp and the file system's support for O_TMPFILE (a three-line test program in the base layer, rudolf-fscheck); fix it in the same start-up repair;

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 15. Flatpak downloads fail with O_TMPFILE on the same installation (stage B)
docs.t: the App Store shows "Linux apps cannot be stored on this computer's data partition: <cause>. See Settings › Apps › Linux › Check." instead of only Flatpak's message. Test. t127d_t.py: after the update, App Store › Linux apps downloads the stand-in Flathub catalogue (qt/mkflat.sh) and installs a small app, as t125_t.py does on a fresh installation.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 16. A Linux self-check (stage B)
docs.t: Settings › Apps › Linux › Check runs rudolf-fscheck and the sandbox start with its reasons. It shows a short list: - the data partition's file system and mount options; - unnamed temporary files (OK or failed); - user namespaces (OK or failed); - the Debian sandbox (started, or failed at <step> with <error>); - Flatpak's repository (folders present and writable). The system report (Task Manager › System, Copy system report / Report a problem) gets the same lines, so a report from a computer like the laptop says what is wrong. Test. tm_t.js: the report has the Linux check lines; t127d_t.py: Check on the repaired installation is all OK.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › Not a bug: web pages drawn by the processor
docs.t: On the laptop, Task Manager says the screen is drawn by the graphics card (radeonsi), while web pages are drawn with SwiftShader (the processor). That is the default: the desktop page renders in software unless Settings › Display Properties › Graphics is set to "Use it for games and the desktop" (session, GLFLAGS). On this AMD laptop that setting is worth trying (one restart). Nothing changes in 1.2.7.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 17. New boot files on an installed drive, keeping its files (stage C)
docs.t: Why. Updates replace the system (kernel and layers, in /persist/os) but never the drive's boot files: the disc image written at the start of the drive by Install here. A drive installed from a disc before 1.2.2 therefore cannot start with Secure Boot on, however up to date it is. Today the only way is to reinstall from a stick, which erases the data partition (files, settings, Flatpak apps, the Debian setup). Found on the Vivobook (item 11). The space problem (measured). Install here puts RUDOLFDATA right after the image, rounded up to 1 MiB:

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 17. New boot files on an installed drive, keeping its files (stage C)
docs.t: | Disc | Image | |------|-------| | 1.1 | 400 MiB | | 1.1.2, 1.2.0 | 446 MiB | | 1.2.2 | 451 MiB | | 1.2.3 to 1.2.4 | 518 to 519 MiB | | 1.2.5, 1.2.6 | 522 MiB | So a 1.2.6 image does not fit in front of the data partition of a drive installed from 1.1 to 1.2.2, the drives that need this most. Moving an ext4 file system's start means copying all of it, which is slow and unsafe on a laptop battery; that is not done. The plan: a boot area that fits, with the full system on the data partition.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 17. New boot files on an installed drive, keeping its files (stage C)
docs.t: The release gets a small boot image (an ISO 9660 image in the same hybrid layout, signed release list, Secure Boot boot files from the release, the start-up script and kernel, no system layers): about 60 MiB. It fits in front of every data partition Install here has made. It is a published release file next to the disc parts.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 17. New boot files on an installed drive, keeping its files (stage C)
docs.t: Before anything is written, the full system of that release is installed into /persist/os (a normal update slot), and a factory copy of the layers goes to /persist/os/factory (needs about 450 MiB free; checked). The start-up script, finding no layers in the boot image, starts the slot, or the factory copy if no slot starts. This keeps "start the version on the drive" working when an update is broken.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 17. New boot files on an installed drive, keeping its files (stage C)
docs.t: Writing. Not over the drive Rudolf OS is running from while it runs: the boot image is staged on the data partition and written by the start-up script at the next start, before the image area is used (the same place as the disc check): written, read back and compared, the data partition's entry put back in the partition table at the same start and size, then a restart. If the comparison fails, it is written again from the staged copy; the staged copy is kept until a start from the new boot area succeeds.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 17. New boot files on an installed drive, keeping its files (stage C)
docs.t: From another drive: Settings › Update and recovery › Install here gets a second choice when the chosen disk already has RUDOLFDATA: "Replace the boot files only (keep files)". The same steps, written directly. Power loss while the boot area is written leaves the drive unable to start, but the data partition is untouched: a stick's Install here › Replace the boot files only repairs it. The page says this before it starts and asks for the charger. Secure Boot: the boot image's boot files are the release's signed ones, so the same rudolf.cer is enrolled once through MokManager.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › 17. New boot files on an installed drive, keeping its files (stage C)
docs.t: Settings › Security › Secure Boot, when the boot files are older (item 11), offers "Get new boot files…" instead of only "Make a USB stick…". Tests. QEMU: a drive installed from the 1.2.0 disc image (446 MiB) and updated, with files, Flatpak's folder and a Debian folder. The boot files are replaced from the running system. The next start writes them; files are still there, info.bootSecure is 1, and with Secure Boot on (test keys enrolled) it starts. The same from a stick (Install here › Replace the boot files only). A write interrupted (QEMU stopped mid-write) leaves RUDOLFDATA intact, and the stick repairs it. A broken slot falls back to the factory copy.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › Risks
docs.t: Memory (item 6): a Worker per kind holds about 30 MB each. Only kinds actually used are started, and a checker idle for 10 minutes is ended. Camera privacy (item 8): the page already grants media access without asking (--use-fake-ui-for-media-stream in the session). With a working webcam that becomes real, so Settings › Privacy gets a "Camera" switch. Web pages that are not part of Rudolf OS ask first, through Chromium's own permission prompt for those sites (the session flag stays for the desktop page only, if Chromium allows it per origin; otherwise the switch is the control). To be settled in stage C before the driver is enabled.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 update plan › Risks
docs.t: Disk space (item 9): joining needs the image's size again in free space. It is checked first, and the parts can be deleted after. The init change runs on every start. The check code only runs with rudolf.check=1, but a syntax error in init would stop every start. Mitigation: sh -n on the host, and every QEMU test starts the new init. The devplug busy mark left behind (a crash while writing) would stop that disk from auto-mounting until the next start. /run is cleared at start, and the trap removes the mark on any exit.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.0 plan: the development link › How it works
docs.t: A Claude session runs in Anthropic's cloud. It cannot open a connection to the laptop, and from the cloud it can reach only a few sites, GitHub among them. The laptop can reach GitHub too. So both sides use a **private GitHub 1. The session writes a command to the repository: cmd/000123.json on the branch link. 2. The laptop asks GitHub every 5 seconds whether cmd/ changed (a conditional request with ETag, which does not count against GitHub's rate limit when nothing changed), fetches new commands, and runs them in order. 3. The laptop writes the result to res/000123.json (and any files, such as a screenshot, under res/000123/). 4. The session reads the result. Commands (cmd/NNNNNN.json):

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.0 plan: the development link › How it works
docs.t: | kind | what it does | limits | |------|--------------|--------| | sh | runs a shell script as root, with a time limit; stdout, stderr and the exit status come back | 10 min default, 60 min at most; 1 MB of output, the rest cut and said so | | screenshot | a PNG of the real screen (rudolfd's screenshot route) | one per command | | get | sends a file from the laptop | 25 MB at most; nothing under /home unless the owner allowed it when switching the link on | | restart | restarts the computer; the link comes back by itself if it was set to stay on across a restart | — | | end | turns the link off | — |

docs.t: Results (res/NNNNNN.json): {id, kind, started, ended, status, stdout, stderr, files[], approved_by}.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.0 plan: the development link › Who has access, and the limits
docs.t: Anyone who can write to the repository can run any command as root on the laptop while the link is on. Testing boot files, drives and the firmware needs root, so the limits are about when and who, not what: Who: the owner, and whoever the owner gives write access to the repository: a Claude session the owner attaches it to, a collaborator the owner adds. GitHub stores the commands and results, as it stores the code.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.0 plan: the development link › Who has access, and the limits
docs.t: The token: a GitHub fine-grained personal access token that can read and write the contents of that one repository and nothing else. The owner makes it on github.com and types it into Settings on the laptop. It is kept report. Revoking it on GitHub ends all access, even if the laptop was lost. Claude never types or handles it. Off by default. Switching it on asks for an administrator's password. It turns itself off after the time chosen when switching it on (1, 2, 4 or 8 hours) and does not stay on across a restart unless that box was ticked (needed for boot tests; it then still ends at the chosen time).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.0 plan: the development link › Who has access, and the limits
docs.t: Always visible. While it is on, a red banner across the top of the screen says "Development link on: commands from GitHub can control this computer", with the time left and End now. It is drawn above every window, including fullscreen games and the login screen. The boot menu and start-up messages say it too after a restart. Ask first (on by default). Each command waits on screen with its text until the owner presses Allow or Refuse; refused commands come back as refused. The owner can untick it when switching the link on, for unattended runs.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.0 plan: the development link › Who has access, and the limits
docs.t: A log on the laptop of every command, its result and who allowed it (Settings › Security › Development link › Log), kept for 30 days. Test computers only. Settings says so when it is switched on: a computer with personal files should not use it. Known limit, said plainly: rudolfd trusts the desktop's administrator prompt, as it does for ending a process or installing Rudolf OS; it cannot check the password itself, because accounts live in the desktop. Any program already running as the desktop user could switch the link on, but only with a valid token, which only the owner has, and the banner would show it.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.1 plan: start from the internal drive
docs.t: 1.4.1 follows 1.4.0 (stable serial 2026102713). Its one goal: a computer where Rudolf OS is installed starts from its own drive, without a USB stick. The ASUS Vivobook Go (E1404FA) cannot today, so it starts through an old 1.1 stick, and Secure Boot cannot be used (the stick's 1.1 start files are not signed).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.1 plan: start from the internal drive › What the development link showed (2026-10-27, commands 000001-000006)
docs.t: The firmware's boot entries: Boot0000 "Windows Boot Manager" and Boot0002 "Ubuntu" (GPT partitions that no longer exist), Boot0003 "UEFI: USB" (the stick), and none for the internal drive. The firmware did not add one by itself. The stick starts as a CD: Boot0003's device path ends in a CD-ROM node (El Torito entry 1). The firmware has never used the image's partition table, on the stick either.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.1 plan: start from the internal drive › What the development link showed (2026-10-27, commands 000001-000006)
docs.t: The internal drive's table is the disc image's hybrid MBR, as Install here copies it: partition 1 (type 0x17, the ISO 9660 file system) starts at sector 0 and contains partition 2 (type 0xEF, the EFI system partition, sectors 0x4C58-0xAC58); partition 3 is RUDOLFDATA. By the UEFI rules for MBR disks (partitions must not overlap), such a table is invalid, and the firmware treats the disk as having no partitions. A boot entry Rudolf OS wrote (Boot0004: HD(2,MBR,0x6ACC513D,0x4C58,0x6000)/\EFI\BOOT\BOOTX64.EFI), used once with BootNext and the stick unplugged: the firmware kept the entry but went to its setup screen. Consistent with the above: it cannot find partition 2.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.1 plan: start from the internal drive › What the development link showed (2026-10-27, commands 000001-000006)
docs.t: The internal drive and the stick have the same MBR disk signature (0x6ACC513D, from the image), so a boot entry naming the drive by signature could also match the stick. The 1.3.1 fix works on the laptop: started through the stick (bootvia=usb), it runs 1.4.0 from the internal drive (nvme0n1p3, slot b).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.1 plan: start from the internal drive › Stage A: what the check on the laptop showed (2026-10-27 evening, commands 000007-000013)
docs.t: The plan was to make the internal drive's table valid by hand and start once from it, before writing code. It did not answer the question, and it taught three things: The stick's 1.1 start-up and the drive share an image ID (rudolf-1.1: the drive was installed from that stick). With partition 1 gone, the 1.1 start-up would mount the whole drive as its media and lock RUDOLFDATA out. So the test also changed the drive's image ID (rudolf-1.T), after backing up the two sectors to RUDOLFDATA

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.1 plan: start from the internal drive › Stage A: what the check on the laptop showed (2026-10-27 evening, commands 000007-000013)
docs.t: Both test starts went through the stick, and the stick's 1.1 start-up then took the stick's own RUDOLFDATA (before, it always found the internal drive's first): the laptop came up as the stick's 1.1 system, without the link. Whether the firmware accepts the corrected table is still unknown. To get the link back, the stick's 1.1 system downloaded 1.4.0 onto the stick's own data, and the link was switched on there.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.1 plan: start from the internal drive › Stage A: what the check on the laptop showed (2026-10-27 evening, commands 000007-000013)
docs.t: The development link replayed every old command in that session: its record of what was done is kept on the data partition, and the stick's had none. The owner allowed them one by one; the two restarts restarted the computer, the sector change stopped at its own check (the drive was no longer as expected) and wrote nothing. Item 6. Command 000013 restored both sectors from the backups (byte for byte), and the laptop starts as before: through the stick, 1.4.0 from the internal drive (slot b), the owner's files.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.1 plan: start from the internal drive › Stage A: what the check on the laptop showed (2026-10-27 evening, commands 000007-000013)
docs.t: So the firmware is checked with 1.4.1 itself (stage C): its start-up handles a drive without partition 1, so a start from the drive gives the real system, and a fallback through the stick still finds the owner's files.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.1 plan: start from the internal drive › Stage B: implementation
docs.t: 2. The installed layout. Written where an internal drive gets Rudolf OS's start files: install.sh (Install here, and Replace the boot files only), after writing the image and RUDOLFDATA's entry; the start-up's "new boot files" writer (initramfs/init), after writing the boot image in front of RUDOLFDATA; this is how an installed drive gets it without being reinstalled (Get new boot files); not mkstick.sh: sticks start as a CD, and they keep the image's hybrid table, so they work on every firmware.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.1 plan: start from the internal drive › Stage B: implementation
docs.t: 3. The start-up (initramfs/init): a drive without partition 1 but with RUDOLFDATA as partition 3 holds the system in its first sectors (the ISO 9660 file system starts at sector 0). Mounting the whole disk would claim it and lock out RUDOLFDATA, so the ISO is mounted read-only through a loop device over the whole disk (a loop device does not claim the disk). One mount_media function for every place that mounts media: find_media, the slot kernel's find_media_given, the kexec failure path. MEDIA stays the disk (/dev/nvme0n1), so disk_of, part3, /etc/rudolf/media and rudolf.mediadev= keep meaning "the start drive".

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.1 plan: start from the internal drive › Stage B: implementation
docs.t: Older start-ups. An update kernel from before 1.4.1 (a rollback to the other slot) would mount a whole disk named in rudolf.mediadev= directly and lock out RUDOLFDATA. So 1.4.1 passes rudolf.mediadev= only for a partition; for a whole disk, the older kernel finds no media, and takes RUDOLFDATA by rudolf.persist=UUID (since 1.3.0). The test covers a rollback to a 1.4.0 slot. Everything that reads /etc/rudolf/media is checked for a whole disk: rudolfd (where it started from), bootfiles.sh, install.sh, mkstick.sh (Make a stick from "this Rudolf OS"), keepfiles.sh. 4. Disk signature. A random signature (bytes 440-443) when the installed layout is written, so boot entries name this drive and not a stick made from the same image.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.1 plan: start from the internal drive › Stage B: implementation
docs.t: 5. Boot entry. After the installed layout is written: a "Rudolf OS" entry (HD(2,...)/\EFI\BOOT\BOOTX64.EFI, shim, so it also works with Secure Boot), first in BootOrder; an older Rudolf OS entry for the same drive is replaced, other entries are left alone. rudolfd already writes EFI variables (Restart into Windows, Prepare Secure Boot); this uses the same code. Without EFI (BIOS starts) nothing is written.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.1 plan: start from the internal drive › Stage B: implementation
docs.t: *As built:* the entry names the drive itself, as the firmware's own drive entries do (PciRoot(0)/Pci(2,2)/Pci(0,0)/NVMe(1,EUI-64) on the Vivobook, or .../Sata(port,0xFFFF,0)), with no partition or file: firmware then starts \EFI\BOOT\BOOTX64.EFI from whatever partitions it found on the drive. The first version named HD(2,MBR,...), and OVMF skipped it at every start: EDK2's partition driver takes the image's El Torito catalogue before the MBR, so no HD(2,MBR,...) node ever exists on that drive (the stick shows the same: its entry ends in a CD-ROM node). The PCI root is named PNP0A03 as EDK2 does, or as the firmware's own entries name it. A controller other than NVMe or SATA still gets the HD(2,...) form.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.1 plan: start from the internal drive › Stage B: implementation
docs.t: on another data partition (or after forgetting it) it started from command 000001 again. Now it also reads which results are already in the repository (res/, one listing per check) and treats every command that has a result as done. A command is only run when it has no result yet.

docs.t: QEMU's firmware (OVMF) starts the hybrid table anyway, so it cannot show the laptop's problem. The QEMU tests check that the installed layout is written correctly and starts: a new t141 (Install here, and Get new boot files on a drive installed from 1.2.0 and on one installed from 1.4.0: the table, the signature, the boot entry and BootOrder in the firmware's variables, a start from the drive by that entry, files kept, an update and a rollback to the older slot); and the usual set (t125, t128b, t130, t131, t140, sb_t, v120). The real check is stage C.

Download rudolf-os-1.4.1-boot.iso and its .sha256; Settings › Security › Secure Boot › Get new boot files. The next start writes them, the installed layout and the boot entry, then restarts. 3. Its path: PciRoot(0)/Pci(2,2)/Pci(0,0)/NVMe(1,EUI 00-26-B7-38-22-72-47-D5)/CDROM(1,0x52EC,0x1E000)/\EFI\BOOT\BOOTX64.EFI: AMI also takes the image's El Torito catalogue. rudolfd's "Rudolf OS" entry names the same drive (same prefix, same EUI byte order) but the firmware skipped it and changed it at every start; 1.4.2 takes the path of the entry the system started from (t141 3b). 5. docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.4: cleanup, the volume and brightness keys, the network indicator, the Settings layout, the screen saver, the taskbar and power saving, and the clock (plan)
docs.t: A pass over everything Rudolf OS builds and ships, looking for code and files that nothing uses (2026-10-30, on 1.4.2). The system programs are clean: no unused functions in iso/sys/*.c (gcc -Wunused-function, and every non-static function is called), and every rudolfd API route has a caller (lsync is called by the script rudolfd injects into the page). What is left is small. 1.4.4 removes it and adds a build check so it does not come back. Nothing a person uses changes by the cleanup. 1.4.4 also makes the volume and brightness keys work (part 2).

docs.t: Desktop (items 1-2). Delete the two definitions; rebuild iso/www/index.html. The cache (item 3). git rm -r iso/sys/root/usr/lib/rudolf/frames/_metadata; iso/.gitignore gets sys/root/usr/lib/rudolf/frames/_metadata/.

docs.h: Part 1: cleanup › How
docs.t: The base layer (items 3-6). The release build copies sys/root over the previous base layer, so files that leave the repository, and programs the full build used to copy, stay in the base layer until removed explicitly. ci_release.sh gets a list of paths to remove from the base layer (systools/base-remove.txt): ` usr/lib/rudolf/frames/_metadata usr/bin/ostree usr/bin/dbus-send usr/bin/dbus-run-session usr/bin/pacat usr/bin/paplay usr/bin/parecord ` Each is removed only if present; the list is part of BSRC, so a change to it rebuilds the base layer. mkrootfs.sh (full builds) stops copying the same programs: dbus-send and dbus-run-session from its D-Bus list, pacat and its links from the sound server's, and ostree from Flatpak's.

docs.h: Part 1: cleanup › How
docs.t: A check that keeps it so (systools/deadcheck.py, run by ci_release.sh before anything is built, and as a host test): every top-level function and arrow function in desktop/*.js is named somewhere else in desktop/ (its own module, another one, or build19.py's patches); every C program in sys/ compiles with -Wunused-function -Werror=unused-function; every file in sys/root is tracked by git (no build output); every program in systools/base-remove.txt is absent from mkrootfs.sh's copy lists. It fails the release build with the name of what is unused, like the duplicate-function check build19.py has had since 1.4.0.

docs.h: Part 2: the volume and brightness keys
docs.t: On the ASUS Vivobook Go, F1 (mute), F2 and F3 (volume down and up), F4 and F5 (brightness down and up) do nothing. Found through the development link (2026-10-30, 1.4.2):

docs.h: Part 2: the volume and brightness keys
docs.t: The keys never arrive. Recording every input device for 40 seconds while they were pressed showed no key events at all. On ASUS laptops these keys are not sent by the keyboard but by the firmware (ACPI WMI events), and the kernel turns them into key presses only with the asus-nb-wmi driver, which Rudolf OS's kernel does not have (kconfig.sh builds none of the laptop platform drivers; only mxm-wmi is there by default). Other makers do the same through their own drivers: Lenovo (ideapad-laptop, thinkpad_acpi), HP (hp-wmi), Dell (dell-wmi), Acer (acer-wmi).

docs.h: Part 2: the volume and brightness keys
docs.t: Nothing would act on them. rudolf-display passes every key below 256 to the X server; the desktop has no handler for the volume keys (XF86AudioRaiseVolume…) or the brightness keys (XF86MonBrightnessUp…). There is no system volume. Settings › Volume Controls sets the desktop's own mix (inside the desktop page); apps with their own sound (Flatpak apps such as Oolite, Linux apps) play through the sound server and do not follow it. The sound server's output on the Vivobook: alsa_output.card1.analog-stereo, at 100 %. Brightness can be set already: rudolfd's brightness?value= writes /sys/class/backlight/amdgpu_bl1 (19005 of 65535, 29 %); only Settings › Display Properties uses it.

docs.h: Part 3: the network indicator
docs.t: On the Vivobook, the taskbar's network icon says "Ethernet — connected", with a wired icon, while the laptop is on Wi-Fi; it has no Ethernet port at all. Found in the code (2026-10-30): The indicator never looks at the real network. netUpd() (desktop, base_v24.html) draws it from the browser version's simulated connections (NETC, saved as bd95net), whose default is one wired connection named "Ethernet", active. On installed Rudolf OS nothing replaces that, so the icon shows the simulated "Ethernet" as connected whenever the browser is online, through whatever network.

docs.h: Part 3: the network indicator
docs.t: The simulation is on Settings › Network Settings too. "Connections" and "Add a connection" (name, type, SSID, security, password, addresses) are the browser version's simulation; on installed Rudolf OS they change nothing, next to the real Wi-Fi and Manual address sections. sit0 is listed as a wired adapter. It is the kernel's IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnel device (IPV6_SIT, on in the default configuration), not hardware; Task Manager shows "sit0 (wired)", and when Wi-Fi was missing, Network Settings showed it as the only network hardware.

docs.h: Part 5: the screen saver
docs.t: Today: one screen saver (a starfield with the time), set only by Settings › User Settings › Screen saver (Off, 2, 5, 10, 15 or 30 minutes), drawn on a page canvas, which Chromium draws with the graphics card. 1.4.4 gives it its own section in Display Properties › Screen saver: Screen saver: On or Off (a saved "Off" or a time from before stays as it was). Start after: 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45 or 60 minutes without input.

docs.h: Part 5: the screen saver
docs.t: Style: eight presets, each with a live preview in the page and Preview (full screen until a key or the pointer moves): 1. Starfield: today's, flying through stars. 2. Clock: a large clock and the date, drifting slowly so it never stays in one place. 3. Rudolf: the Rudolf OS logo bouncing off the screen edges, changing colour at each bounce. 4. Code rain: falling columns of characters. 5. Mystify: two outlines of joined lines that bounce and change colour, leaving trails. 6. Bubbles: soft bubbles rising and drifting. 7. Aurora: slow bands of colour waving across a night sky. 8. Fireworks: rockets bursting into falling sparks. Show the time: over any style except Clock (on by default).

docs.h: Part 5: the screen saver
docs.t: Ask for the password when it ends (from User Settings; Lock stays there).

docs.h: Part 5: the screen saver
docs.t: Drawn by the processor. Each style draws into a canvas made with `getContext('2d', {willReadFrequently: true})`, which Chromium keeps in memory and draws with the processor (Skia's software renderer) instead of on the graphics card; no WebGL, no CSS animations or filters. To keep the processor's load small: at most 30 frames a second, at most 1280 pixels wide (larger screens show it scaled up), no drawing while it is hidden. Only the finished picture goes to the screen, as everything on the desktop does. The page test checks that every style makes its canvas this way (and none other), and measures its frame time in a CPU-only Chromium.

docs.h: Part 5: the screen saver
docs.t: When it starts. As now, not while something is full screen, the mouse is captured or media plays. On installed Rudolf OS the time without input comes from rudolf-display, which sees every key and pointer movement, also in games and Linux apps (the desktop page sees only its own), so it never starts over a game being played; rudolfd's idle gives the milliseconds since the last input. In the browser version, as now.

docs.h: Part 6: the taskbar's clock, quick settings and battery; power saving
docs.t: Checked in the code (2026-10-30): The calendar shows another time than the taskbar. The taskbar clock (clk2, base_v24.html) uses the time zone set in System Settings (S.tz) and the 24-hour setting (S.h24). The calendar that opens from it (shell25.js) formats the time and date with toLocaleTimeString([], …), without either: Chromium's own zone and format. With a time zone set, the two differ by hours (and the calendar may mark the wrong day as today); with 24-hour on, they differ in format. The lock screen and the screen saver's clock do the same as the calendar.

docs.h: Part 6: the taskbar's clock, quick settings and battery; power saving
docs.t: Quick settings (the ☰ panel) has a volume and a brightness slider besides the toggles, and the battery as a line of text at the bottom. The taskbar already has its own volume control (the 🔊 icon and its popup); brightness has none. There is no power management beyond "Sleep after" (in User Settings): no power modes, nothing for the lid, the screen is never turned off, no battery saver. Task Manager on the Vivobook lists two batteries: the laptop's (45 %, charging) and a second one at -1 % (a device that reports a battery it does not have).

docs.h: Part 6: the taskbar's clock, quick settings and battery; power saving › Items
docs.t: Power and battery: Battery: the level, charging or not, the time left or to full, its health (capacity now against new, from energy_full/energy_full_design) and charge cycles, when the battery reports them. Power mode: Power saver, Balanced (the default) or Performance. It sets the firmware's platform profile (/sys/firmware/acpi/platform_profile: low-power, balanced, performance; ASUS laptops have it through asus-nb-wmi, part 2) and the processors' energy preference (energy_performance_preference of amd-pstate or intel_pstate: power, balance_performance, performance), whichever the computer has. Separate choices on battery and when plugged in.

docs.h: Part 6: the taskbar's clock, quick settings and battery; power saving › Items
docs.t: Battery saver: on now, or on by itself at 10, 20 or 30 % (or never); off by itself when the charger is plugged in. While it is on: Power saver mode, the screen 30 % dimmer (not below 10 %), the desktop's animations and transparency reduced, the screen saver at 10 frames a second, update checks and the app catalogue refresh waiting until it is off, and Wi-Fi power saving on (iw dev wlan0 set power_save on). The battery icon shows a leaf while it is on.

docs.h: Part 6: the taskbar's clock, quick settings and battery; power saving › Items
docs.t: Turn the screen off after: Never, 1, 2, 5, 10, 15 or 30 minutes without input, on battery and plugged in (rudolf-display: DPMS off on Xorg, the framebuffer blanked on the software display; any input turns it back on). Sleep after (from User Settings): Never, 5, 10, 15, 30, 60 minutes, on battery and plugged in. When the lid is closed: Sleep, Turn the screen off, or Do nothing, on battery and plugged in (rudolf-display reads the lid switch, which it ignores today, and writes lid closed/lid open to the events; rudolfd acts). When the power button is pressed: Ask (the Shut down dialog, as now), Sleep, or Shut down.

docs.h: Part 6: the taskbar's clock, quick settings and battery; power saving › Items
docs.t: Battery care (where the firmware supports it: charge_control_end_threshold, ASUS and others): stop charging at 60, 80 (recommended when the laptop is mostly plugged in) or 100 %. Each choice is kept on RUDOLFDATA (/persist/etc/power.conf) and applied by rudolfd at every start and whenever the charger is plugged in or out, so it holds without anyone signed in.
