docs.h: Part 7: the clock sets itself
docs.t: Found on the Vivobook (2026-10-30, 1.4.2): its clock had gone back to 2016-01-01 (the hardware clock reset, most likely when the battery ran flat). Every HTTPS connection then failed ("SSL peer certificate or SSH remote key was not OK", since no certificate is valid in 2016): updates could not be checked and the development link could not switch on. Rudolf OS sets the clock from the internet only when someone presses Settings › Network Settings › Clock › Set the clock from the internet (rudolfd time/sync, BusyBox ntpd, which needs no certificates); it did, and all worked again.

docs.h: Part 7: the clock sets itself
docs.t: | # | What | Where | |---|---|---| | 33 | Never earlier than the release. At start, before anything uses the network, rudolf-init sets the clock to the running release's build date when it reads earlier than that (the date written into the base layer when it is built, /usr/share/rudolf/released; a clock cannot honestly be older than the system it runs). | iso/sys/root/sbin/rudolf-init | | 34 | From the internet by itself. rudolfd sets the clock with ntpd (pool.ntp.org, then time.google.com) once the network is up after a start, at each wifi connected and when a wired link comes up, and every 12 hours; the result goes to the hardware clock (hwclock -w -u). An HTTPS failure about a certificate while the clock is more than a day off what the time servers say is retried after the sync. | iso/sys/rudolfd.c | | 35 | The button stays, in System Settings › Date, time and language › Clock (part 4), with the last automatic sync shown next to it ("set from the internet at 18:59"). | desktop/ |

docs.h: Part 7: the clock sets itself › Release
docs.t: Branch rudolf-1.4.4, after 1.4.3 is out. Version 1.4.4. The kernel is rebuilt (item 7), so the release carries a new kernel and modules. The changes list: "New: the volume and brightness keys work on laptops (ASUS, Lenovo, HP, Dell, Acer), with an on-screen indicator, and Settings › Volume Controls has the system volume. Fixed: the taskbar said Ethernet was connected on computers using Wi-Fi. New: eight screen savers, drawn by the processor, set in Display Properties › Screen saver. Changed: Settings is reorganised (each page and what moved). Fixed: the calendar showed another time than the taskbar. Fixed: the clock now sets itself from the internet, and never falls back before the release (a reset clock broke updates). New: the battery and brightness on the taskbar; power modes, battery saver, screen off, the lid and the power button, and battery care in System Settings › Power and battery. Removed unused programs and code." A beta, the checks above, promote; no disc needed.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.4.5: SpreadsheetPro and PresentPro, the Cyberdeck test removed, "Open settings…", and shutting down and restarting quickly (plan)
docs.t: What 1.4.5 adds and changes (asked for 2026-11-01, on 1.4.4): Part 1: the Cyberdeck test mode is removed. Part 2: the desktop's right-click item "Change background…" becomes "Open settings…". Parts 3 and 4: two companion apps to WordPro: SpreadsheetPro, in the place of Excel, and PresentPro, in the place of PowerPoint. They replace the small Spreadsheet and Presentations apps that Rudolf OS has had since 1.2. Part 5: Shut down and Restart are checked, measured and made to finish quickly. The 1.4.4 updates waiting to be merged come first and are not part of this plan: #59 (one network icon) and #60 (a picture as the desktop background). The Fn-lock fix (#58) is already merged.

docs.h: Part 5: shutting down and restarting quickly
docs.t: What happens now. The desktop, when Shut down or Restart is chosen: saves the open files (fsFlush, the home folder's encryption homeChain); saves the session and the local storage copy; plays the shutdown sound; calls rudolfd. None of these steps has a time limit; if one stalls, the dialog stays at "Please wait…". rudolfd's power?action=poweroff|reboot then: asks the desktop's Chromium to close, and waits up to 25 seconds for it; kills it; finishes keeping the files of a live session, if that applies; runs sync and umount -a -r; powers off or restarts.

docs.h: Part 5: shutting down and restarting quickly
docs.t: The browser window for sign-in sites (RudolfWeb, when it is open), Linux apps, the sound server, Wi-Fi and the development link are not asked to close. /persist (also mounted as the home folder) is not made read-only before umount -a -r, so a program still writing to it can keep it from being unmounted cleanly. Checked on the Vivobook (2026-11-01, 1.4.4, through the development link): The last start found /persist clean: no journal recovery, so today's shutdown does finish its job. What runs at shutdown: the desktop's Chromium, which also holds Oracle's real tabs (11 processes), the sound server (PulseAudio), D-Bus, Wi-Fi (wpa_supplicant, udhcpc), rudolf-portal, rudolf-display, Xorg and the development link. Restart: the kernel's reboot method is acpi, mode cold.

docs.t: What is slow, then, is most likely the waiting (the desktop's steps and up to 25 seconds for Chromium), not the disk. Item 28 measures it before anything is changed.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.0: security
docs.t: 1.4.x made the system hard to tamper with (Secure Boot with Rudolf's own key, signed modules, dm-verity on the read-only system layers, signed A/B updates with fallback). 1.5.0 closes the gaps that are left, without growing the system by more than a few megabytes, and adds remote access.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.0: security › 1. Firewall (incoming connections)
docs.t: Kernel: NF_TABLES with NF_TABLES_INET, NFT_CT, NFT_REJECT, NFT_LOG built in (checked in kconfig.sh). nft (and its libraries, about 1 MB) in the root file system. /usr/lib/rudolf/firewall loads the rules at start-up, before the network is up: - incoming: allow loopback, replies to connections the computer made (ct state established,related), DHCP replies, ICMP needed for the network to work (ping replies, too big, unreachable); count and drop the rest. - outgoing: everything is allowed. - remote access opens its port (8443) only while it is on, and only from the local network (private addresses). Settings › Security: the firewall on/off (administrator), how many incoming connections it blocked since start-up.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.0: security › 1. Firewall (incoming connections)
docs.t: The desktop's URL rules for Oracle tabs were called "Firewall"; they become Website blocking (they did not change).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.0: security › 2. System health log
docs.t: The Report a problem dialog and its system report already exist (docs/system-reports.md). 1.5.0 adds a record of what happened over time, kept on the computer: /persist/var/log/health.log, one JSON line per event, at most 512 KB (the older half is dropped when full). Events: start-up (how long it took, which slot), slot fallback after an update, memory guard closing a page, crash of the desktop or the browser, Debian program crash, sign-in failures, disk nearly full, high temperature, firewall blocks (counted per hour, not one line each), remote-access sessions (who, from which address, how long). Settings › System › System health: the events, newest first, and a summary (start-up time, crashes this week).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.0: security › 2. System health log
docs.t: The system report includes the last 50 events (account names and addresses left out, like the rest of the report). Nothing is sent anywhere. The permanent machine ID (/persist/etc/machine-id, for D-Bus) is never in the log or the report.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.0: security › 3. Administrator access to account files
docs.t: Today each home folder is encrypted with a key made from its own password: nobody else can open it, and an administrator resetting a forgotten password leaves the user with an empty home folder. Each account gets a random file key (AES-256-GCM). The home folder is encrypted with it. The file key is stored wrapped: - with a key made from the account's password (PBKDF2-SHA256, 210 000 rounds, as now); administrator's password; any account's file key is wrapped for every administrator's public key, so this works when the administrator is not signed in. Administrators can open this account's files: a switch per account (Settings › Accounts), on by default. Turned off, the administrator copies of that account's key are deleted.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.0: security › 3. Administrator access to account files
docs.t: File Explorer: an administrator sees C:\USERS\<name> of the other accounts and can open them. An administrator resetting a password re-wraps the file key: the files stay. Existing homes move over at the account's next sign-in. Honesty: the welcome file and Settings say that administrators can open the account's files (or that they cannot, when the switch is off). Not covered: the Linux side (Debian, Wine) has one Linux home for every account, as before.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.0: security › 4. Data encryption
docs.t: The system layers stay as they are (signed, verified, unencrypted): start-up, updates and fallback do not change. Data is encrypted with the kernel's own file encryption (fscrypt on ext4, FS_ENCRYPTION, AES-256-XTS for contents and AES-256-CTS for names): no extra partition, no cryptsetup. /persist/vault is an encrypted directory. Debian (/persist/debian), Flatpak apps (/persist/flatpak) and files kept in Downloads move into it. One random data key for the computer. It is wrapped for every account with that account's password (as the file keys above), and with a recovery key shown once when encryption is turned on (to write down or save).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.0: security › 4. Data encryption
docs.t: Unlock: the first sign-in with a password after start-up unlocks the vault (rudolfd adds the key to the kernel); Guest does not unlock it. Linux and Flatpak programs wait until it is unlocked ("Sign in to an account to use Linux programs"). Settings › Security › Encrypt my data: administrator, shows the recovery key, moves the data over as a job with progress (needs free space as large as the largest folder that moves), then deletes the unencrypted copies. New installs format RUDOLFDATA with the encrypt feature; existing ones get it with tune2fs -O encrypt while mounted (no restart: checked on a loop device, the kernel sees the feature at once).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.0: security › 4. Data encryption
docs.t: Not encrypted: the browser profile (the desktop's own data in it is already encrypted per account), settings, logs. A USB stick with Rudolf OS unlocks on any computer with the password (no TPM binding in 1.5.0).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.0: security › 5. Remote access
docs.t: A remote desktop in any web browser, served by Rudolf OS itself. certificate (EC P-256, made on first use), a viewer page, and a WebSocket that sends the screen (changed tiles, deflate) and takes keyboard and mouse input (XTest, as rudolf-display). Off by default. An administrator turns it on in Settings › Remote access, which shows the address (https://<ip>:8443) and a pairing code (6 digits, new every time it is turned on). Signing in from the viewer: the pairing code (once per browser, remembered by a cookie), then a Rudolf OS account and its password (checked against the same PBKDF2 hashes as the sign-in screen). Five wrong tries lock it for a minute.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.0: security › 5. Remote access
docs.t: Approval: someone at the computer must Allow the session; a marker stays on screen while someone is connected, with a button to end it. Unattended access: per account, set by an administrator. That account can connect without approval, so the computer can be reached when no one is there. The firewall opens 8443 only while remote access is on, and only to the local network. Access from outside (WireGuard) is for a later version. Every session goes into the health log.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.0: security › Size
docs.t: nft and libraries ~1 MB, rudolf-remote ~60 KB, viewer ~20 KB, desktop modules ~40 KB. fscrypt needs only the kernel.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.0: security › Tests
docs.t: iso/qt/shell2/: Settings pages, admin access to homes (wrap/unwrap, reset keeps files, switch off), Website blocking. iso/qt/sb/t150*: in QEMU: firewall blocks an incoming connection and allows replies; health log after start-up; encryption: turn on, restart, locked until sign-in, Debian works after unlock, recovery key unlocks; remote access: viewer signs in, approval, screen arrives, input works, firewall closes 8443 when off.

A restart in the middle of Make a USB stick had twice left a stick without its system.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.3: devices without a driver, and USB Wi-Fi › 0. Devices without a driver (the base for the rest)
docs.t: Today, a part with no driver shows nothing. Nobody can tell whether it is missing or broken. rudolfd GET devices/unsupported: each PCI, USB and I2C/ACPI device that no driver claimed, with its ID and what kind it is (Bluetooth, sound, camera, Thunderbolt, Wi-Fi, other). Settings › Devices: Not supported yet, the list in plain words ("Intel Bluetooth (8087:0033): no driver yet"). The system report (Report a problem) includes the list. Then a report from any laptop says what that laptop is missing. Health log: one hardware line at the first start-up on a computer, with what it found.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.3: devices without a driver, and USB Wi-Fi › 7. USB Wi-Fi adapters: Ralink and MediaTek RT2800 (found on the Vivobook, 2026-11-07)
docs.t: What was found (Development link, commands 126-129, read-only): The adapter is a Ralink RT5370 USB Wi-Fi dongle (148f:5370, "802.11 n WLAN"). It is a USB 2.0 device, so it runs at 480 Mbit/s (high speed) in any port. A SuperSpeed port cannot make it faster, and Rudolf OS reports that speed correctly. Rudolf OS does not recognize it. No driver claimed it, no network interface appeared, and Settings › Network shows only the built-in Wi-Fi (wlan0, rtw88_8821ce).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.3: devices without a driver, and USB Wi-Fi › 7. USB Wi-Fi adapters: Ralink and MediaTek RT2800 (found on the Vivobook, 2026-11-07)
docs.t: Cause 1: the driver is silently left out of the kernel. iso/kconfig.sh asks for RT2800USB as a module, but RT2800USB depends on the RT2X00 menu, which is not switched on. make olddefconfig drops it without a word. The RT5370's ID is also behind RT2800USB_RT53XX, which is not set either. Of the Wi-Fi drivers the file asks for, rt2800usb is the only one missing on the Vivobook (mt7922e is not a real driver: the MT7922 is handled by mt7921e). Cause 2: its firmware is not included. rt2800usb loads rt2870.bin for every chip it drives, and iso/firmware-extra.txt does not have it.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.3: devices without a driver, and USB Wi-Fi › 7. USB Wi-Fi adapters: Ralink and MediaTek RT2800 (found on the Vivobook, 2026-11-07)
docs.t: The port: the Vivobook Go E1404FA's firmware describes the port the dongle is in (usb3-port3) as having **no SuperSpeed partner**, unlike usb3-port1 and usb3-port2, which pair with usb4-port1 and usb4-port2 (10 Gbit/s). So according to the laptop itself, that port is a USB 2.0 port. For a USB 2.0 dongle it makes no difference. Settings should still show it (below), so the question has an answer on screen. Why nothing said so: kconfig.sh checks the hotkey, Bluetooth and memory options after olddefconfig, but not the Wi-Fi drivers. And a device with no driver shows nothing anywhere: section 0 is for exactly this. The fix:

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.3: devices without a driver, and USB Wi-Fi › 7. USB Wi-Fi adapters: Ralink and MediaTek RT2800 (found on the Vivobook, 2026-11-07)
docs.t: Kernel (iso/kconfig.sh): - y RT2X00 (the menu: it only makes the drivers selectable); - m RT2800USB with every chip family: RT2800USB_RT33XX, RT2800USB_RT35XX, RT2800USB_RT3573, RT2800USB_RT53XX, RT2800USB_RT55XX, RT2800USB_UNKNOWN. That covers the RT2770, RT2870, RT3070, RT3071, RT3072, RT3370, RT3572, RT3573, RT5370, RT5372 and RT5572, the chips of most inexpensive USB Wi-Fi dongles sold since about 2010; - m RT2800PCI with RT2800PCI_RT33XX, RT2800PCI_RT35XX, RT2800PCI_RT53XX (the same chips as PCIe cards in older laptops; same firmware family, rt3290.bin for the RT3290); - remove MT7922E from the list (not a real option); - after olddefconfig, check every Wi-Fi module the file asks for (as is done for Bluetooth): the build fails if any of them was dropped. Then this cannot happen silently again.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.3: devices without a driver, and USB Wi-Fi › 7. USB Wi-Fi adapters: Ralink and MediaTek RT2800 (found on the Vivobook, 2026-11-07)
docs.t: Firmware (iso/firmware-extra.txt): rt2870.bin (8 KB) and rt3290.bin (4 KB) from linux-firmware, pinned by SHA-256 and checked against the copy the CI build fetches, as with Realtek Bluetooth (#80, #81). The older rt73.bin and rt2561*.bin chips (RT73USB, RT61PCI) are left out: they are 802.11g from before 2008.

docs.t: Settings › Network, more than one Wi-Fi adapter: - today the Wi-Fi panel and start-up use the first adapter found (wifi.sh firstif), so a dongle next to the built-in Wi-Fi would never be used; - with two or more, the panel gets an Adapter choice ("Built-in: Realtek RTL8821CE" / "USB: Ralink RT5370"), passed to rudolfd as if= (api_wifi already accepts it); - the choice is saved (/persist/etc/wifi-adapter, by MAC address, since USB names change between ports); at start-up wifi.sh boot uses the saved adapter when it is plugged in, otherwise the first one; - unplugging the adapter in use falls back to the built-in Wi-Fi by itself, with a notification.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.3: devices without a driver, and USB Wi-Fi › 7. USB Wi-Fi adapters: Ralink and MediaTek RT2800 (found on the Vivobook, 2026-11-07)
docs.t: Settings › Devices, USB: each USB device with its speed in plain words ("USB 2.0, 480 Mbit/s"), the port's own speed ("USB 3 port, 10 Gbit/s", from the port's SuperSpeed partner), and its driver or "no driver yet". It shares its code with section 0. Tests: Host: the kconfig check fails a configuration where a requested Wi-Fi driver was dropped; wifi.sh with two stand-in adapters picks the saved one, and falls back when it is gone. Browser test: the Adapter choice appears only with two or more adapters, and is passed on.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.3: devices without a driver, and USB Wi-Fi › 7. USB Wi-Fi adapters: Ralink and MediaTek RT2800 (found on the Vivobook, 2026-11-07)
docs.t: On the Vivobook: - the RT5370 appears (rt2800usb, wlan1 or similar), scans and joins the home network; - choose it in Settings and restart: it is used again; unplug it: the built-in Wi-Fi takes over; - the built-in RTL8821CE and the Realtek Bluetooth are unchanged; - Settings › Devices shows the dongle as "USB 2.0, 480 Mbit/s" and the port it is in as USB 2.0 (and a SuperSpeed port as USB 3, 10 Gbit/s). Size: about 0.2 MB in the modules layer (rt2x00lib, rt2800lib, rt2800usb, rt2800pci and two firmware files).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam
docs.t: These parts of the 1.5.3 plan were moved here when 1.5.3 was released (stable 1.5.3.261108, serial 2026110803). 1.5.3 shipped the list of devices without a driver, USB Wi-Fi adapters with RT2800 chips and a choice of Wi-Fi adapter, and fixes found while installing Rudolf OS on the HP desktop (docs/plan-1.5.3.md). 1.5.4 adds support for the hardware most other laptops have: Bluetooth from Intel, MediaTek and Qualcomm, and Bluetooth built into the board (UART); sound on laptops from about 2020 on; Windows games on Steam through Proton; Thunderbolt and USB4 docks; the built-in cameras of newer Intel laptops; the Library's remaining follow-ups.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam
docs.t: The kernel stays at 6.18, which has the drivers all of this needs. Drivers and firmware go only into the modules layer, like 1.5.1's Bluetooth, so the system layer barely grows. Each firmware file comes from linux-firmware, pinned by its SHA-256 in iso/firmware-extra.txt (fwextra.py). The CI build fetches exactly the files pinned there (#101) and checks each hash. Every driver asked for in kconfig.sh is checked after olddefconfig, as the Wi-Fi drivers are since #99, so none is dropped without a word.

docs.t: The drivers for Intel and MediaTek (BT_INTEL, BT_MTK) are already in the kernel. Only their firmware is missing.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 1. Bluetooth: Intel, MediaTek, Qualcomm and built-in UART
docs.t: Choosing the firmware: fwextra.py gets a mode like wififw.py's: take the files the built Bluetooth modules ask for (MODULE_FIRMWARE), and the newest older version where an exact one is missing. CHANGELOG: Bluetooth "on computers with an Intel, MediaTek, Qualcomm or Realtek chip". Tests: - The host test checks the chosen firmware list against the modules. - QEMU: with a stand-in Bluetooth controller (-device usb-bt-dongle where QEMU has it, or a virtual HCI), the adapter appears and Settings works. - On the Vivobook (Realtek): nothing changes. - Intel, MediaTek and Qualcomm can only be tested on hardware with those chips. See "Testing" below.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 2. Sound on newer laptops
docs.t: The kernel has only the classic HDA driver. It plays sound on the Vivobook, but many laptops since about 2020 send their speakers or built-in microphones through a sound processor (DSP). Without its driver they have no sound, or no microphone. Intel (SOF), Tiger Lake to Lunar Lake: - kernel: SND_SOC, SND_SOC_SOF_TOPLEVEL, SND_SOC_SOF_PCI, SND_SOC_SOF_INTEL_TOPLEVEL, and the platforms (Tiger Lake, Alder Lake, Raptor Lake, Meteor Lake, Lunar Lake). Also the generic machine driver (sof-hda-dsp), SND_SOC_DMIC, and SoundWire (SOUNDWIRE_INTEL with its machine driver); - SND_INTEL_DSP_CONFIG chooses HDA or SOF per computer, as other systems do; - firmware: intel/sof-ipc4/, intel/sof-ace-tplg/ and intel/sof-tplg/ for those platforms only (10–15 MB: the largest addition; the older Skylake to Ice Lake platforms stay on HDA).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 2. Sound on newer laptops
docs.t: AMD (ACP): - kernel: the digital microphones of Renoir, Cezanne, Rembrandt and Phoenix (SND_SOC_AMD_RENOIR, SND_SOC_AMD_ACP6x and SND_SOC_AMD_PS with their machine drivers), and SOF for AMD (SND_SOC_SOF_AMD_TOPLEVEL) where a laptop uses it; - the Vivobook may well use one of these for its microphone: it is the first test. Speaker amplifiers (without them the speakers stay silent or very quiet, though headphones work): - Cirrus CS35L41 and CS35L56 (many ASUS, Lenovo and HP laptops): SND_HDA_SCODEC_CS35L41_I2C/SPI, SND_HDA_SCODEC_CS35L56, firmware cirrus/ for the listed laptops; - TI TAS2781 (Lenovo): SND_HDA_SCODEC_TAS2781_I2C, firmware ti/tas2781/. The sound server: - DSP sound cards need ALSA's UCM profiles: alsa-ucm-conf (1 MB) goes into the root file system; - PulseAudio 16.1 is checked to load them (module-alsa-card with UCM).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 2. Sound on newer laptops
docs.t: Settings › Sound shows the microphone and its level, and what kind of sound card was found ("Intel sound processor (SOF)"), so a report says it. Tests: - in the host test, the chosen firmware is checked against the modules; - on the Vivobook: the speakers, the headphone jack, the built-in microphone (before and after), HDMI sound; - in QEMU: HDA as today (no change). Intel SOF can only be tested on hardware. As built (#107; this PR): the AMD microphones (no firmware) first, then Intel SOF, the amplifiers, UCM and sound hotplug:

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 2. Sound on newer laptops
docs.t: Intel SOF firmware comes from thesofproject/sof-bin (linux-firmware has none), pinned by iso/firmware-sof.txt (fwextra.py sof): 11th–13th generation use IPC3, the kernel's default for them, from SOF 2.2 (the last IPC3 release; topologies 2.2 to 2.2.13); Core Ultra uses IPC4 from SOF 2.15 (topologies 2.15.1; intel/sof-ace-tplg is a link to intel/sof-ipc4-tplg). Intel-signed only, about 27 MB unpacked, 1.8 MB compressed. Panther Lake and Wildcat Lake came along (6.18 has them). AMD SOF is left out: linux-firmware and sof-bin have no firmware for Renoir, Rembrandt, Van Gogh or ACP 6.3 (only amd/sof/acp7f, for a newer ACP 7 part). AMD SOF is used mostly by Chromebooks and the Steam Deck; other AMD laptops use the ACP microphone drivers (#107).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 2. Sound on newer laptops
docs.t: alsa-ucm-conf comes from the build machine (Ubuntu 24.04). PulseAudio uses it for every card but plain HD Audio (use_ucm=0 there), so the Vivobook's speakers, headphones and HDMI are set up as before. sound hotplug (mdev, snd/controlC*) opens a card in PulseAudio when it appears and closes it when it goes. Found by 1.5.3's "Not supported yet" list: the Vivobook's AMD audio processor (ACP, 1022:15e2) has no driver. It most likely carries the built-in microphones, so the ACP part of this section can be tested on the Vivobook itself.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 3. Steam and Proton
docs.t: Steam is in the App Store's Games tab since 1.2.5, as a Flatpak from Flathub (unverified, so an administrator allows it). It has never been tried with Windows games through Proton on Rudolf OS. 1.5.4 makes that a supported, one-click path. 1.5.2 already did the window part: Windows games in Wine get the keyboard properly (WM_TAKE_FOCUS) and cover the whole screen when they go full screen (#95, #96, tested with Starport GE on the Vivobook). Proton runs games the same way, so this applies to them too. Still to do:

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 3. Steam and Proton
docs.t: The kernel: - NTSYNC (/dev/ntsync, used by recent Proton versions; readable by the user); - vm.max_map_count = 1048576 (some games need it); - the open-files limit for the session raised to 524288 (Proton's esync). Controllers in Steam: - /dev/uinput and the controllers' /dev/hidraw* usable by the signed-in user (mdev.conf). Then Steam Input works for Xbox, PlayStation and Switch controllers, by USB and by Bluetooth. 32-bit graphics: - installing Steam also installs Flathub's 32-bit graphics runtime (org.freedesktop.Platform.GL32.default) that matches the Flatpak runtime; - Proton needs Vulkan. Steam's card says "Needs a graphics card with Vulkan" and warns on computers that draw with the processor or have no Vulkan driver (old Intel graphics before Broadwell, NVIDIA older than the cards NVK supports).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 3. Steam and Proton
docs.t: Game mode: Steam's Big Picture and full-screen games already hold notifications (1.5.1). Steam is added to the apps that count as gaming, so the screen does not lock while a controller is used. Where games are kept: - in Steam's Flatpak folder on the data partition (inside the encrypted folder when "Encrypt my data" is on); - the App Store says how much space is free, and Steam's "add a library folder" works for a second drive (Flatpak permission for /media).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 3. Steam and Proton
docs.t: Anti-cheat: - games whose anti-cheat supports Proton (Easy Anti-Cheat and BattlEye, when the developer turned it on) work; - the others (for example Valorant, Fortnite, Call of Duty) do not, and nothing tries to get around their anti-cheat; - Steam's card says this in one line, and points to cloud gaming for those.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 3. Steam and Proton
docs.t: Tests: - On the Vivobook: install Steam, sign in (you), and run with Proton: - one free Windows-only game, for example a free-to-play title; - one game with Easy Anti-Cheat that supports Proton; - full screen, the keyboard and switching away and back (Super+Tab), as with Starport GE. - Check controller input by Bluetooth and USB, sound, game mode, and the frame rate against the same game on Windows if you have it. - Browser test: Steam's card and its warnings on a computer without Vulkan. As built (this PR):

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 3. Steam and Proton
docs.t: kernel: NTSYNC and HID_STEAM built in; HID_PLAYSTATION was asked for but dropped without a word (it needs LEDS_CLASS_MULTICOLOR), so PlayStation 4 and 5 controllers had only hid-generic: fixed, and every controller and games option is checked after olddefconfig; rudolf-init: vm.max_map_count 1048576, and the hard open-files limit 524288 (Wine raises its own soft limit to it; the soft limit stays 1024 for everything else); mdev: /dev/uinput and /dev/ntsync for the desktop user; /dev/input/event* only for game controllers (joyperm, the same test as udev's input_id), so apps cannot read the keyboard;

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 3. Steam and Proton
docs.t: appextra: Steam gets --filesystem=/media (library folders on drives) and org.freedesktop.Platform.GL32.default for its runtime's branch, after the install, after Update all, and (as a job) the first time a Steam installed earlier is opened; Steam's card: Vulkan (from the graphics driver and glamor's renderer), anti-cheat, free space; game mode: rudolf-display's window list says which windows are full screen, and notifications wait while one is in front. Not done: Steam's games stay in ~/.var/app/com.valvesoftware.Steam on the data partition, outside the encrypted folder. Moving ~/.var there as a link, as Downloads is, may not work inside Flatpak's sandbox, and a bind mount at sign-in has not been tried: both need trying on the Vivobook first.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 4. Thunderbolt and USB4
docs.t: Basic USB-C works today: USB devices, and charging that the hardware does by itself. Docks, displays through Thunderbolt or USB4, and devices that need PCIe over the cable do not. Kernel: - USB4 (the thunderbolt driver), HOTPLUG_PCI_PCIE, PCIEPORTBUS; - TYPEC, TYPEC_UCSI, UCSI_ACPI (USB-C ports: which end powers which, and the modes); - TYPEC_DP_ALTMODE (displays over USB-C), DisplayPort tunnelling over USB4 in amdgpu and i915/xe; - the IOMMU for both makers (INTEL_IOMMU, AMD_IOMMU), turned on by default, so a device on the cable cannot read memory it was not given. Check first that kconfig.sh has them. Network chips in docks: ATLANTIC (Aquantia, in many Thunderbolt docks). Realtek USB and Intel I225 are already in.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 4. Thunderbolt and USB4
docs.t: Approving a device (/usr/lib/rudolf/thunderbolt, rudolfd /api/tb): - When the firmware reports DMA protection (iommu_dma_protection = 1), devices are approved by themselves, as Windows and macOS do it. - Otherwise a new device asks: "Allow CalDigit TS4? Only allow docks and devices you trust." Only an administrator can answer, from the same kind of question box as Bluetooth pairing. - Approved devices are kept by their unique ID (/persist/etc/thunderbolt-allowed) and approved again when they are plugged in. Settings › Devices lists the Thunderbolt and USB4 devices, approved or not, with Forget.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 4. Thunderbolt and USB4
docs.t: Tests: - host test of the script against a stand-in /sys/bus/thunderbolt: approval, refusal, devices kept and approved again when plugged back in, the automatic approval with DMA protection; - on hardware: a dock (display, network, USB), and a USB-C display on the Vivobook if its port supports DisplayPort. As built (this PR): kernel: USB4, TYPEC, TYPEC_UCSI, UCSI_ACPI, TYPEC_DP_ALTMODE, TYPEC_TBT_ALTMODE, USB_ROLE_SWITCH (built in, or UCSI can only be a module), PCIEPORTBUS, HOTPLUG_PCI_PCIE, INTEL_SCU_PCI with TYPEC_MUX_INTEL_PMC, INTEL_IOMMU, AMD_IOMMU, and AQTION (the option is called that, not ATLANTIC), all checked after olddefconfig; DP tunnelling (DRM_DISPLAY_DP_TUNNEL) comes with i915;

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 4. Thunderbolt and USB4
docs.t: the Intel IOMMU is not forced on for every computer (INTEL_IOMMU_DEFAULT_ON stays off, as in the defconfig): the kernel turns it on by itself where the firmware asks for DMA protection, which is what makes iommu_dma_protection 1, and forcing it on everywhere can break older Intel graphics; /usr/lib/rudolf/thunderbolt (mdev for SUBSYSTEM=thunderbolt, and at start-up), rudolfd GET tb, tb/ask, POST tb/allow, tb/deny, tb/forget; "no" holds until the device is unplugged; the system report has the list; tb54.js: the question box, and the section in Settings › Devices.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 5. Built-in cameras on newer Intel laptops (preview)
docs.t: USB cameras (UVC), in nearly every AMD laptop and older Intel ones, already work in Oracle. Intel laptops since Tiger Lake often have a MIPI camera behind Intel's IPU6, or IPU7 on Lunar Lake. These need a driver for the processing unit, one for the camera sensor, and an image processor in software. Kernel: - VIDEO_INTEL_IPU6, plus IPU7 if 6.18 has it; - INTEL_SKL_INT3472 (the camera's power and LED); - the common sensors: OV2740, OV01A10, OV02C10, OV08X40, OV13B10, HI556; - firmware intel/ipu/. libcamera with its software image processor (the "simple" pipeline), about 3 MB.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 5. Built-in cameras on newer Intel laptops (preview)
docs.t: Getting the picture to Oracle: Chromium reads cameras through V4L2, which libcamera cameras are not. Two ways, to be chosen after a prototype: - (a) v4l2loopback, built and signed with the kernel's modules. A small rudolf-camera turns the built-in camera into an ordinary V4L2 camera while a page uses it, started and stopped by rudolfd when Oracle asks for the camera (the permission prompt already exists); - (b) libcamera's V4L2 compatibility layer loaded into Oracle's camera process. Smaller, but Chromium's sandbox may not allow it. Privacy: - the camera light (INT3472) is on whenever the camera is; - Settings › Privacy shows which page is using the camera; - nothing runs while no page asks for the camera.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.4: more hardware, and Steam › 5. Built-in cameras on newer Intel laptops (preview)
docs.t: Off by default in 1.5.4: Settings › Devices › Built-in camera › Try the new camera support. It is turned on by itself in a later update once it has worked on a few laptops. Not included: infrared face-recognition cameras (Windows Hello), and fingerprint readers (a later release). Tests: - host test of the start and stop by rudolfd, with a stand-in; - the Vivobook's USB camera in a video call (nothing changes); - an IPU6 laptop for the rest. As built (this PR; the kernel part only, chosen on 2026-11-08 because no computer here has an IPU6 camera to try libcamera and the way to Oracle on):

docs.t: kernel: VIDEO_INTEL_IPU6, VIDEO_INTEL_IPU7 (staging), IPU_BRIDGE, INTEL_SKL_INT3472, Intel's Visual Sensing Controller (INTEL_VSC, INTEL_MEI_VSC, in front of the camera on many Alder Lake and Meteor Lake laptops), and the sensors OV2740, OV01A10, OV02C10, OV02E10, OV08X40, OV13B10, OV5675, HI556, HI846, all modules and checked after olddefconfig (with MEDIA_PCI_SUPPORT, without which IPU6 was dropped); firmware: intel/ipu/ipu6*_fw.bin and ipu7*_fw.bin (2.8 MB); devplug lists an IPU6 or IPU7 with its driver in "Not supported yet" ("driver ready, apps cannot use it yet"); still to do, on a laptop with such a camera: libcamera with its software image processor, choosing (a) or (b) below, the camera light and Settings › Privacy, and the switch in Settings › Devices.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.5: file management
docs.t: Released as stable 1.5.5.261108 (serial 2026110820) on 2026-11-08, with disc-1.5.5. It is the first disc image published as one file (#113). It shipped with: item 1, Downloads for each account (#117); the fixes found on the Vivobook: - the Trash's tooltip, and adding and removing desktop icons (#114, #121); - every file in Downloads showing (#115); - the AMD microphones (#118); - Downloads after a restart, held downloads, endless "Downloading…" and wrong addresses (#119). Items 2–7 below moved to docs/plan-1.5.6.md, to be built on the disk. 1.5.4 is stable (1.5.4.261108, serial 2026110815, with disc-1.5.4). 1.5.5 has already started with fixes found on the Vivobook: the Trash's tooltip (#114); adding and removing app shortcuts on the desktop, with Desktop icons… (#114);

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.5: file management
docs.t: every file in the Downloads folder showing in File Explorer (#115). This plan covers the rest of 1.5.5, File Explorer and storage, in the order of the stages at the end. What is there today, checked in the code before writing this: Your files on drive C: live in the desktop's own storage (IndexedDB, mirrored by rudolfd). Each account's home folder (C:\USERS\<name>) is encrypted with that account's file key (1.5.0). Shared with Linux apps: Documents, Pictures, Downloads and Games are also folders on the disk (/home/rudolf/…), kept in step with C:. One Linux user holds them for every account.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.5: file management
docs.t: Downloads (since 1.2.7) are in C:\DOWNLOADS, one folder for all accounts, outside the encrypted homes. Files over 1.5 MB stay on the disk in /home/rudolf/Downloads, and C:\DOWNLOADS holds an entry pointing at each. With "Encrypt my data", that disk folder is inside the encrypted folder. It is still shared by every account. Sorting: the details view sorts by name, date, type or size when a column heading is clicked; folders come first. The icons and thumbnails views have no way to sort, and the order resets to name in every new window or tab.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.5: file management
docs.t: Search: the box searches the current folder, or "Everywhere" below it (file names, and the text inside text files). It stops at 300 results. Drives and the disk's Downloads are not searched. Favourites: folders only. Settings › Storage and backup: the desktop storage used, your home folder, Empty the Trash and the backup. Nothing about the disk itself: Linux apps, Steam games, Debian, Downloads on the disk. The Trash: each item records when it was deleted (t). It has no size shown and no automatic emptying.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.5: file management › 1. Downloads for each account
docs.t: The problem: Every account sees and can delete every other account's downloads. A child's account sees an administrator's. Small downloads (1.5 MB or less) are stored in C:\DOWNLOADS, outside the encrypted home folders. The change: Each account gets its own Downloads again: C:\USERS\<name>\DOWNLOADS, encrypted with the account's file key like the rest of the home folder. - File Explorer's Downloads and Oracle's "Downloaded" notification point there. - The guest's Downloads is not kept after sign-out, like the guest's other files (its home is never saved).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.5: file management › 1. Downloads for each account
docs.t: On the disk, a folder per account: /home/rudolf/Downloads/<account id>/ holds the large files. Entries point into it, and rudolfd's dl/link and dl/read stay inside Downloads as today. The dl/home adoption (#115) looks only in the signed-in account's folder. Who gets a download: - A download goes to the account that was signed in when it finished. - If nobody is signed in, it waits in .incoming and goes to whoever signs in next. Today it went into C: before C:'s files were loaded, which is how entries were lost (#115).

Tests: - browser test with two accounts and the guest: a download goes only to the account signed in; the guest's downloads are gone after sign-out; the move from C:\DOWNLOADS with one account and with two; - host test of rudolfd's per-account folders: no path outside Downloads, no ..; - QEMU t150: the move into the encrypted folder still covers Downloads. docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk
docs.t: Item 8 of the file management recommendations (2026-11-08). 1.5.5 refines File Explorer (docs/plan-1.5.5.md); 1.5.6 changes where your files are kept. On a computer with a RUDOLFDATA partition (installed, or a USB stick with one), every account's home folder becomes real files on that partition. Drive C: becomes the desktop's view of them. The version that runs in an ordinary web browser, and live sessions without RUDOLFDATA, keep today's storage.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › How it works today (checked in the code)
docs.t: Drive C: is one tree of JavaScript objects (fs) in the desktop page: - folders are objects; - text files are strings; - other files are data: URLs (base64, about a third larger than the file). Saving: fsSave() (73 calls across the apps) schedules fsFlush() 300 ms later. It writes two kinds of record: - fs:system: C: without the homes, in IndexedDB; - each signed-in account's whole home folder as one record, home:<id>. homeSave serialises the home to one JSON string, encrypts it with the account's file key (AES-GCM, 1.5.0) and writes it.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › How it works today (checked in the code)
docs.t: So one changed letter in Notepad re-encrypts and rewrites every file in that home. The bigger the home, the slower each save, and the closer to the browser's storage quota. rudolfd mirrors those records on the disk (/home/rudolf/.rudolf-idb), so the shell and the plain page share them. Large downloads (over 1.5 MB, 1.2.1) cannot fit in that record. They stay on the disk as files (/home/rudolf/Downloads/.accounts/<id>/, 1.5.5), and C: holds an entry pointing at each (rudolfdisk:). Viewers read them in pieces through /dlf/ links. This is the only part of C: that is real files today.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › How it works today (checked in the code)
docs.t: Linux apps see Documents, Pictures, Downloads and Games in /home/rudolf/.... lxSync (linux26.js) copies files back and forth between those folders and C:. Two copies, kept in step. "Encrypt my data" (1.5.0) encrypts the disk folders for Debian, Flatpak apps and Downloads with the kernel (fscrypt, /persist/vault). Each account's home is encrypted by the desktop instead. Two encryption systems. Administrators can open accounts' files (acct50.js): every account's file key is also wrapped for each administrator. Backups zip every record (still encrypted).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › What changes
docs.t: One copy of every file, as a real file: - opening and saving touch only that file; - no size limit beyond the disk; - no base64; - no 1.5 MB rule for downloads. Linux apps, Steam, Wine and the desktop see the same folders. No copying in either direction. One encryption system: - each account's folder is encrypted by the kernel (fscrypt) with the account's own file key; - the key is put into the kernel when the account signs in and taken out when it signs out; - administrators' access works as today, through their wrapped copy of the key. Storage, search, duplicates and backup work on the disk directly. rudolfd, du, find.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › Stage 1, as built
docs.t: rudolfd home/* in iso/sys/rudolfd-home.inc, included by rudolfd.c. The folder is /persist/accounts/<id>, not /persist/home/<id>: /persist/home/rudolf is already the Linux user's home. - Requests: GET home, unlock (with session=1 for the binds), lock, tree, list, stat, read (ranges), write (base version, new, pieces with part=1 and final=1, mkdirs=1), mkdir, rename (replace=1), copy, delete. - Every path is walked with openat(O_NOFOLLOW). A key that another open account uses is never taken out. The binds cover Documents, Pictures, Music and Videos only. Downloads joins them in stage 4, when Chromium's .incoming moves out of /home/rudolf/Downloads; otherwise the bind would hide it. Not yet: watch (inotify) comes with stage 2, where the desktop uses it.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › Stage 1, as built
docs.t: Test: host homeapi_t.sh, 27/27, on a real ext4 drive with the encrypt feature (a loop device): - the folder is made with the key's policy, and another account's key is refused; - after lock the names and contents can't be read, also by root; - paths, links, conflicts, pieces, rename, copy and delete; - the binds.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › Stage 2, as built
docs.t: New desktop module home56.js. It decides which accounts keep their files on the disk: an account whose first sign-in is on 1.5.6, on a computer whose RUDOLFDATA supports encryption (USER.disk). - Sign-in: the folder is opened with a 64-byte key made from the account's file key (HKDF-SHA512), with the Linux binds (session=1). - Loading: files up to 1.5 MB are loaded, as text or data: URLs, the way C: keeps them. Larger files become rudolfdisk: references into the account's folder, which open through home/link like large downloads. - Saving: homeSave compares with the snapshot and writes only what changed: new folders, new or changed files (with their base version), copies of references, and deletions (top-most only). - Large downloads in the account's Downloads move in with home/adopt. - Conflicts: a file another program changed meanwhile is kept, and the desktop's version is saved beside it as "… (desktop copy)". - Other programs' changes: the tree is read again every 15 s instead of using inotify. A watch can replace the poll later. - Sign-out: pending writes finish, then the folder is locked.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › Stage 2, as built
docs.t: rudolfd: - home/link: /dlf/ links that hold home:<acct>:<path> and are walked again at every request, so a link a Linux app swaps in can't redirect them; - home/adopt: from Downloads, the account's own folder or the top only, copied across file systems. Not yet for these accounts: backup, an administrator opening their files, and the Trash on the disk (stage 4). The CHANGELOG says so. Tests: browser home56_t.js 20/20; host homeapi_t.sh 30/30. acct50, files, Downloads, stick and desktop tests are unchanged.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › Stage 3, as built
docs.t: hdMove in home56.js. An account from before 1.5.6 (it has a home record, or a file key) moves 1.5 s after signing in, in the background, while it keeps working: 1. the folder is opened without the binds; 2. every folder is made and every file written (replace for what an earlier attempt left); large downloads move in with home/adopt, and references already in the folder are kept; 3. everything is read back, comparing each file's SHA-256 (and the size of moved downloads) and each folder; 4. only then: USER.disk, USER.oldHome (the date), the snapshot from what was written (so changes made during the move are written next), and the binds. - Progress shows every 200 files or 5 s. - A failure leaves everything as it was, says so, writes an event, and is tried again at the next sign-in.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › Stage 3, as built
docs.t: The old record home:<id> is no longer written after the switch, so it stays as it was at the move. It is deleted at the first sign-in after 7 days. Tests: browser home56m_t.js 12/12: - a failed read-back changes nothing; the move at the next sign-in; - text, pictures and empty folders; a 3 MB download moved, not copied; - read-back before binds; the old record kept, then deleted after 7 days; - one write after the move, nothing moved again. home56_t.js (20/20) now turns supported off while its pre-1.5.6 account signs in.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › Stage 4, as built
docs.t: The Trash: - something put in the Trash that holds large files (references) is renamed into the account's .Trash/<stamp>/ on the disk instead of deleted, and the Trash's entries are pointed there (hdTrashRepoint); - Restore renames it back (move), not a copy; - .Trash/<stamp> folders nothing points at any more are deleted after the Trash changes (hdTrashSweep); - small files stay in the Trash's own record, as before. Backup: backupBlob first writes the signed-in account's home as the record backups always had (encrypted with the file key). Large files are not in it, as large downloads never were.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › Stage 4, as built
docs.t: A restored backup: - rudolfd's home/unlock now answers "made" when it made the folder; - a disk account whose folder was just made, but which has a record (a backup restored here, or the account on another computer), is filled from the record by the stage 3 move. Administrators: acOpenHome opens a disk account's folder with its file key (home/unlock without binds, key from hdKeyHex(f, o.id)). acSaveOthers writes its changes with hdSyncFor, and acClose writes and locks it. hdSync is generalised to hdSyncFor(acct, home, snapshot).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › Stage 4, as built
docs.t: Not done in stage 4, each needing the Vivobook: - Downloads stays out of the Linux binds, because Chromium's .incoming would move with it; done after stage 4: the downloads store (.incoming, .quarantine, .accounts, Linux apps' old files) has its own bind, /run/rudolf/dl, made by rudolfd before the account's binds; Chromium's policy points there; Downloads joins the binds; lxSync copies nothing; the copies at the store's top are removed or moved in (hdDlTop); - the Encrypt my data page's wording; - watch (the 15 s re-read stays).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › Stage 4, as built
docs.t: Tests: - browser home56r_t.js 11/11: large files through the Trash and Restore, emptying, small files, the backup record, a restore on a new folder, an administrator opening, changing and locking; - host homeapi_t.sh 30/30 ("made", then "unlocked"); - home56_t, home56m_t, acct50, files, Downloads and desktop tests unchanged.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 1.5.5's remaining items
docs.t: 1.5.5 was promoted on 2026-11-08 with plan items 1 (Downloads for each account) and the fixes found on the Vivobook. Its items 2–7 (sorting, favourite files, storage, the Trash, search, batch rename and duplicates) move here, after stage 4, and are built on the disk directly. Storage, search and duplicates get simpler that way, and the Trash becomes .Trash/ from the start.

What it is: the app's name, version, publisher and size where the file says (a .deb's control fields, an .exe's version information), and where it will be installed. 2. docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › Added on 2026-11-09: installing apps from files, and the camera › Each file type
docs.t: .deb (Debian packages): rudolf-debian deb FILE copies the file into Debian and installs it with apt-get install, which fetches what it depends on. The app's launcher appears in the Start menu, with its own icon. Uninstall: apt-get remove, from Settings › Apps › Linux. .exe and .msi (Windows): the wizard runs the installer with Wine (wine or wine msiexec /i). docs.t: .AppImage: kept in a Programs folder of the account (~/Applications), made runnable, and given a Start-menu launcher with the icon from inside it (--appimage-extract of the .desktop file and the icon only). It runs in Debian, which has the libraries AppImages expect; one that needs FUSE runs with --appimage-extract-and-run. .bin (Linux installers): these are programs that install something else (drivers, games, tools); what they do differs for each one. The wizard shows what the file is (file), warns that it runs with the account's rights in Debian, and runs it in a Terminal window, where its own questions can be answered. Not as administrator.

docs.t: The device (#136): cameras (video*, media*, v4l-subdev*) belong to the video group the desktop is in. Checked on the Vivobook after the fix: the Camera app (photos and video), Oracle's websites asking for the camera (the shell's permission prompt), Discord's video calls (Flatpak, which has the device), and Settings › Privacy › Camera off and on. docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 1. Where the files go
docs.t: ` /persist/accounts/<account id>/ one per account, encrypted with its file key (fscrypt v2, AES-256-XTS) Desktop/ Documents/ Pictures/ Music/ Videos/ Downloads/ .Trash/ the account's Trash (files, and where each came from) .rudolf/ the desktop's notes on files (comments, favourites, sort orders) /persist/accounts/guest/ tmpfs, emptied at sign-out (as the guest's home is today) ` C:\USERS\<name> is that folder. The other parts of C: (Programs, the system folders) stay in fs:system: they are small and the same for everyone. Names keep their case on the disk. The desktop's names are upper case today. The view shows a file as it is named, and compares names without case, so Report.pdf and REPORT.PDF are one file (a second one is Report (2).pdf).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 1. Where the files go
docs.t: While an account is signed in, /home/rudolf/Documents, Pictures, Downloads, Music, Videos and Games are bind mounts of that account's folders. Every Linux app (Flatpak, Debian, Wine, Steam) sees that account's files. Nothing is mounted while nobody is signed in.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 2. rudolfd: files in the homes
docs.t: A new file API (home/*), only inside /persist/accounts/<the signed-in account> (and an administrator's opened account): list, tree, stat: names, folder or file, size, modified time, a version number (mtime and size) for "changed elsewhere". read (with ranges, for viewers and the antivirus) and link (as /dlf/, for <video> and PDFs). write: whole file or appended chunks, then an atomic rename. It refuses a write whose base version is out of date (the file changed meanwhile), and the desktop asks which copy to keep. mkdir, rename, move, copy (a job when large), delete (into .Trash/), purge. watch: changes made by Linux apps (inotify), passed on as events, so File Explorer and open apps update.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 2. rudolfd: files in the homes
docs.t: Path checks: absolute paths built by rudolfd from the account and a relative path. No .., and no links leading out. Keys: POST home/unlock (the account's file key, sent once over the local API after the desktop unwraps it) adds the fscrypt key and mounts the binds. home/lock removes the key and unmounts them, at sign-out and at switch-user.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 3. The desktop: C: as a view
docs.t: The apps keep using the in-memory tree (node(), d[name]=value, fsSave()), so they need no changes: At sign-in, the home's tree is read from the disk (tree): names, sizes, times. A file's content is read when it is first opened. Small text files (under 256 KB) are read at once in the background, so search and previews do not wait. A file not read yet is a reference, as downloads are today, generalised from rudolfdisk: to every file. Opening it reads it. Viewers that already read references in pieces (video, PDF, images) keep doing so.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 3. The desktop: C: as a view
docs.t: Saving: - fsFlush() no longer writes the home as one record. It compares the tree with the last version written (strings are compared by identity first, which costs nothing when unchanged) and writes only files that changed, made or went away, through home/write, mkdir, rename and delete; - a crash or power cut loses at most the last 300 ms, as today, and never a whole home; - renames and moves inside C: are found from File Explorer's own operations (cut, paste, rename, drag), which call rudolfd directly rather than going through the comparison.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 3. The desktop: C: as a view
docs.t: Changes from outside (a Linux app saved a file): watch events update the tree. If the file is open and edited in the desktop, the app is told and asks: keep mine, or reload. The rest of C: (fs:system), the browser-only version and live sessions without RUDOLFDATA keep the current storage, unchanged.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 4. Moving the homes (once, at an account's first sign-in on 1.5.6)
docs.t: 1. The desktop decrypts the home record as today. 2. It writes every file to /persist/accounts/<id>/, which is already encrypted. Large downloads (the .accounts/<id>/ files) are moved, not copied. 3. It reads the tree back and compares names, sizes and SHA-256s with the record. 4. Only then does it switch to the disk. It keeps the old record for the update fallback: if 1.5.6 does not start twice in a row, the computer goes back to 1.5.5, which still has the old record. Files changed after the move would then show their old version in 1.5.5. The notification says so, and the record is deleted once 1.5.6 has been the working system for 7 days. Other cases:

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 4. Moving the homes (once, at an account's first sign-in on 1.5.6)
docs.t: A home that cannot be moved (a full disk, a damaged record) stays as it is, with a notification and a health-log line. Nothing is lost, and the move is tried again at the next sign-in. C:\SHARED DOWNLOADS (BEFORE 1.5.5) moves to /persist/accounts/shared-downloads/, readable by every account, if it is still there. Progress is shown, because a large home takes a while: "Moving your files to the disk… 1,234 of 5,678 files".

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 5. What changes with it
docs.t: Downloads: - Oracle's checked downloads move straight into the account's Downloads/; - the 1.5 MB split, the rudolfdisk: entries, the reconcile and the adoption (#115, #117) go away; - .incoming and .quarantine stay. "Encrypt my data": - Debian and Flatpak stay in /persist/vault; - Downloads leaves it, because it is now inside each account's own encrypted folder; - the setting says that homes are always encrypted, and that "Encrypt my data" covers Linux. The Trash is .Trash/ in the account's folder: restoring is a rename, and its size comes from the disk. 1.5.5's Trash items move with the home. Storage, search and duplicates (1.5.5 items 4, 6, 7) use rudolfd on the disk. Search can read every file.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 5. What changes with it
docs.t: Backup: - "Back up everything" makes one archive of every account's folder, read through the keys of the accounts that are signed in. Accounts that are not signed in are copied with their fscrypt-encrypted names and contents, which restore only onto this computer's RUDOLFDATA. The page says so, and offers a backup per account, decrypted, for another computer; - restoring older backups (records) goes through the move in item 4. Administrators opening an account's files (acct50) adds that account's key while the administrator has the folder open, and removes it when they close it. The guest: a tmpfs home, as now. Settings › Storage shows homes as real sizes on the disk.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 6. Risks, and how each is handled
docs.t: Losing files in the move: - it copies, verifies with SHA-256, and keeps the old record for 7 days; - QEMU tests move homes of 10 and 5,000 files, and one with a damaged record. An app that writes a file the desktop has open: versions on every write, and the app asks when they differ. Speed: opening a file is a local HTTP call to rudolfd (milliseconds). Listing a folder of 10,000 files is measured in the QEMU test and must stay under 1 s. fscrypt on older drives: the encrypt feature is added to RUDOLFDATA as "Encrypt my data" does today (tune2fs -O encrypt). A drive that cannot take it (not ext4) keeps today's storage, and says so.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 6. Risks, and how each is handled
docs.t: Two people's files in Linux apps: the bind mounts change at sign-in. An app left running from the previous account is stopped at switch-user, as Linux apps are today when the account changes. Going back to 1.5.5: covered for 7 days by the kept record (item 4). After that, a fallback to 1.5.5 would see an empty home. The update keeps 1.5.6 from falling back past 7 days, and says so.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 7. Tests
docs.t: Host: rudolfd's home/* against a temporary ext4 image with the encrypt feature (root): - paths that try to leave the folder; - versions and conflicts; - unlock and lock (the files unreadable after lock); - bind mounts. Browser (stand-in rudolfd with a disk in memory): - the view; - only changed files written; - references read on open; - outside changes; - the move with verification and a damaged record.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 7. Tests
docs.t: QEMU t156: - a 1.5.5 home with documents, pictures and a large download, updated to 1.5.6: files on the disk, encrypted after sign-out, readable after sign-in; - a Linux app (busybox in Debian) sees and edits a document, and the desktop shows the edit; - the fallback to 1.5.5 within the 7 days shows the old home; - a backup and its restore; - two accounts, an administrator opening the other's files. The Vivobook: your real home moved; Oracle, Steam, Emu, Notepad, WordPro, Paint and the Linux apps on the same files.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 8. The last change before release: one Start button
docs.t: Moved from the 1.5.7 plan (its Part 3, item 7) on 2026-11-10. This, and any fixes it needs, are the last changes before 1.5.6 is released.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 8. The last change before release: one Start button
docs.t: One button for the logo and the version (asked for on 2026-11-10, for 1.5.7; moved here the same day). The taskbar has the logo (Start) and, right beside it, "Rudolf OS 1.5.6" (#osver, misc25.js), which opens Settings › About: two buttons next to each other that both lead into the same place. They become one button: the logo with "Rudolf OS" and the version beside it, in one frame, that does only what the Start button does (a click opens the Start menu, a right-click its menu, and the keyboard and screen readers know it as "Start"). Settings › About stays where it is, in Settings and the Start menu. On a taskbar at the left or the right (150 px wide) the text goes under the logo, or is left out when it does not fit. The screen saver and About's picture take the logo from it as before.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 8. The last change before release: one Start button
docs.t: The whole version number, whatever it is (asked for on 2026-11-10): the text is the full version as the system has it (RVER, from the release's version), never a fixed "1.5" or a pattern of three one-digit parts. It must show 1.5.7, 1.10.0, 1.12.15, 2.0 and 10.3.1 whole; the button's width follows the text, and only the side taskbars may leave the text out, never cut it. Anything that compares versions (the update check, "what's new", the Library's minimum versions) compares them part by part as numbers (1.10.0 is newer than 1.9.9), and a test covers these versions.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.6: your files on the disk › 8. The last change before release: one Start button
docs.t: Built in 1.5.6: misc25.js (the version is a part of the Start button, .stv; the second button is gone), styles25.css (beside the logo at the bottom and the top, under it at the left and the right, on two lines there if need be, never cut), core25.js verCmp (versions part by part as numbers; What's new lists them newest first with it; nothing else compares versions today: updates go by the release's serial, and the Library has no minimum versions yet). Test: iso/qt/shell2/startbtn56_t.js.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught
docs.t: Asked for on 2026-11-09, after the Vivobook tests of the 1.5.6 betas. 1.5.6 finishes first (its installation wizards, the camera, the Terminal and 1.5.5's remaining File Explorer items); this plan starts once 1.5.6 is promoted. Four parts: 1. Blitzen diagnostics: Blitzen reads the computer's own state and Rudolf OS's documents, and explains what went wrong, without changing anything. 2. Recommended improvements: what the 1.5.6 betas showed on real hardware: a deleted download, a wrong path, a setting lost between requests, a browser restarted after sleep. Each led to a fix; these make the next ones less likely, and quicker to find.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught
docs.t: 3. Apps, games and start-up (added on 2026-11-09, after Steam and Among Us on the Vivobook): stopping apps, saying what the memory guard did, the network at start-up, and what 1.5.6 leaves for later. (Three more found that day went into 1.5.6 itself: prompts in front of full-screen games, installer windows hidden behind the desktop, and Chromium's own shortcuts that could close the desktop.) 4. WebKit for the desktop, Chromium only for browsing (added on 2026-11-10): the desktop and its built-in apps run in WebKit, a lighter web engine, so that they take much less of the memory; Chromium stays, as the web browser, started only to browse.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › What is there today (checked in the code and on the Vivobook)
docs.t: Blitzen (1.3.x, blitzen26.js) is the offline assistant: a small model run by llama.cpp (rudolf-ai, started on demand by rudolfd), with a context of 8,192 tokens by default. It answers about code (BlockLua, Lua, Luau, Pilot.lua, JavaScript, C++, Python) with context packs (blitzpacks26.js): short reference cards, each under about 800 words, sent with a question. "Ask Blitzen" is in Notepad, the Code Editor, BlockLua Builder and the Terminal. The Vivobook (the test computer): Ryzen 3 7320U, 3.4 GB of memory, about 1.2 GB used with the desktop open. A model that fits beside the desktop has about 1 to 3 billion parameters.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › What is there today (checked in the code and on the Vivobook)
docs.t: What the computer records about itself: - the health log (/persist/var/log/health.log, System health): start-ups, crashes, the browser restarted, sign-in failures, the encrypted folder; - rudolfd's log (/run/rudolf/rudolfd.log, lost at restart), session.log, the job log of the last task; - the system report (tm26.js sysReport, "Report a problem"): version, hardware, drivers, storage, network; - the hardware check (hwcheck30): keyboard, touchpad, camera, battery, screen; - the desktop's own events (logEvt, Event Viewer), which stay in the desktop's storage.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › What is there today (checked in the code and on the Vivobook)
docs.t: What could not be seen during the 1.5.6 tests: - the desktop's errors were to go to /run/rudolf/page.log (/api/clientlog), but no page.log was ever written on the Vivobook, also when the 1.5.6 Downloads clean-up should have reported; - rudolfd's log is gone after a restart.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › Part 1: Blitzen diagnostics › What it does
docs.t: "Why?" next to what failed: - a notification of an error ("Your files could not be opened", an install that failed); - a line of the health log or the Event Viewer; - the installation wizard's failure, the Terminal's last command. "What's wrong with this computer?" in System health: Blitzen reads the latest problems and says, in plain words: - what happened and when; - the likely cause, with the log line it comes from; - what to do: a setting to change, something to install, or "report it" when it is a fault in Rudolf OS.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › Part 1: Blitzen diagnostics › What it does
docs.t: "Draft a report": the problem, the steps, the system report and the relevant log lines in one text, for the person to read and send (Report a problem, or to the developers). Nothing is sent by Blitzen.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › Part 1: Blitzen diagnostics › What it reads (read-only)
docs.t: Rudolf OS's documents, as reference material found by search, not training: - the CHANGELOG (what changed in which version, and the known fixes); - the plans in docs/ (how each part works: the disk, Downloads, the wizards, encryption, updates); - the Help pages and the Settings search entries. Kept with the release as a small index (/usr/share/rudolf/blitzen-docs), split into sections of about 300 words, and searched by words (BM25) before each question. The best few sections go with the question: the model's context is small, so only what matters is sent.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › Part 1: Blitzen diagnostics › What it reads (read-only)
docs.t: This computer's state, through a new rudolfd endpoint ai/facts that only reads: - the health log (last 100 lines), rudolfd's log, session.log (filtered: no passwords, tokens or keys), the last job's log; - the system report; - the desktop's events (sent by the desktop with the question); - the hardware check's last result. The person sees what is sent to the model ("Blitzen will read: …") and can remove lines first. It all stays on this computer, as Blitzen already does.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › Part 1: Blitzen diagnostics › What it does not do
docs.t: No changes: Blitzen does not run commands, change settings, install, delete or move files. It suggests; the person does it (with a button to open the right page when there is one). Anthropic's terms do not allow training a general assistant on Claude's outputs without written permission, and this plan does not: the documents are searched, not trained on. No promises it cannot keep: answers say how sure they are, and quote the log line they rest on. When nothing in the logs explains a problem, it says so and offers the report.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › Part 1: Blitzen diagnostics › Size and speed on the Vivobook
docs.t: The index of documents: about 2 MB, searched in the desktop in under 100 ms. An answer of a few sentences from a 1 to 3B model on 4 cores: about 10 to 30 seconds. The answer streams as it comes. When memory is short (a game, a large page), Blitzen says it will answer when there is room, as today.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › Part 1: Blitzen diagnostics › Tests
docs.t: Host: ai/facts filters secrets (a test log with a token, a password line and a key) and reads only the files it lists. Browser (a stand-in model that echoes what it received): the right sections and log lines are sent for a known failure; nothing is sent without the person seeing it; no button runs a command. On the Vivobook: three real problems from the 1.5.6 betas (a download not found, a package not readable, sleep restarting the browser), asked as the person would ask. The answer must name the right cause or say it does not know.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › Part 2: recommended improvements
docs.t: From the 1.5.6 betas on the Vivobook, in order of how much each would have helped. 1. Nothing deleted by a background task without a way back. Two downloads were deleted by Linux apps' two-way copying (fixed in #133). Deletions that no person asked for (sync, clean-ups, reconciles) go to a recovery folder for 7 days instead (.Recovered in the account's folder, shown in the Trash with "Restore"), and the health log says what went there and why. 2. The desktop's events and errors on the disk. Find why page.log was never written on the Vivobook (the shell frame, the token, or the page), fix it, and write the desktop's Event Viewer to the account's folder too, so the (/persist/var/log/rudolfd.log.1…3).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › Part 3: apps, games and start-up
docs.t: Found on 2026-11-09 with Steam (Flatpak) and Among Us (Proton) on the Vivobook. 1. Ending an app from Task Manager. Steam stuck half-closed (its window gone, its process left) could only be (all their sandboxes as one, from /run/user/N/.flatpak, as the memory guard counts them since 1.5.6), Debian's Linux apps and Wine programs, also those with no window open (Discord in the tray). "End" asks the app to quit, then ends it after 5 s; a rudolfd endpoint apps/end does it as root, for that app's processes only.

And before a full-screen game starts while little memory is free and background apps are open: "Discord is running in the background and uses 600 MB. Close it for the game?"

The same for everything the desktop fetches at start-up: the update check, the App Store's lists, Oracle's home page and Blitzen's packs wait for the network (rudolfd's network state, and the online event) or try again soon, instead of failing once and waiting for the next turn.

The windows come from the display server itself (a short client, no new package: the computer has

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › Part 3: apps, games and start-up
docs.t: 5. Memory in System health (asked for on 2026-11-09). A Memory section in Settings › System health, beside Power and battery: - Compressed memory: Automatic (as large as the memory, at most 8 GiB, as since 1.5.6; recommended), Smaller (half of it, as before 1.5.6) or Off. No free size: too small runs out sooner, too large spends the computer's time compressing. A change applies at the next restart (shrinking a full one would stall the computer); the rudolf.nozram=1 start-up option stays, and wins. Kept in /persist/etc/rudolf-memory, read by /usr/lib/rudolf/memory, set through a rudolfd endpoint memory/settings (administrators). - Now: memory in use, and how much is compressed and how full it is (as Task Manager shows). - What the memory guard closed in the last 7 days, from the health log (on 2026-11-09 a Newgrounds Flash game's page at 1,882 MB; Discord, when it is closed as a background app), each with its time and size. - "Close apps with no window open when memory runs out", on by default (the memory guard's rule since 1.5.6).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › Part 4: WebKit for the desktop, Chromium only for browsing
docs.t: Asked for on 2026-11-10, after the comparison with Ubuntu and Mint: of the ways to make the desktop lighter, this one needs the least work for the largest gain.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › Part 4: WebKit for the desktop, Chromium only for browsing › Why
docs.t: On the Vivobook (3.4 GB) the desktop's own Chromium takes about 780 MB (its main process, the desktop page, the graphics process, the network process), and more with web pages open. With Steam, Discord and a game, that is what ran out: the white screens and the watchdog's restarts of 1.5.6 (#160, #167) came from it. The desktop and every built-in app (File Explorer, the Office apps, Settings, the App Store, the emulators, Blitzen) are web code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, WebAssembly). A native desktop (Xfce, LXQt, Qt or GTK) would mean writing them all again; another web engine runs them as they are.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › Part 4: WebKit for the desktop, Chromium only for browsing › Why
docs.t: WebKit (WPE WebKit with its small launcher Cog, or WebKitGTK) is the engine of GNOME's Web and of many devices' screens; it usually takes noticeably less memory per page than Chromium. How much less on the Vivobook is measured first (step 1), before anything is changed.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › Part 4: WebKit for the desktop, Chromium only for browsing › What changes
docs.t: The desktop page (the desktop, the taskbar, the Start menu and every built-in app) runs in Cog (WPE WebKit), in place of the Chromium kiosk. The session starts it the same way, in the desktop's memory group (#160), with the same watchdog (its heartbeat is the same request to rudolfd). Web pages (Oracle Browser, the links in apps, sign-in pages, Newgrounds, cloud gaming) open in Chromium, as a separate window: started when someone browses, closed when its last window is. Today they open in tabs inside the desktop (the shell's Controlled Frames); they become Chromium's own windows and tabs, with Rudolf OS's policies (downloads into the account's Downloads, the camera prompt, the keyboard shortcuts of #151).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › Part 4: WebKit for the desktop, Chromium only for browsing › What changes
docs.t: What only Chromium has, and what replaces it: - the shell (an Isolated Web App with Controlled Frames): not needed by the desktop any more; the web pages are Chromium's own windows (above); - the Ruffle extension (Flash in web pages): Flash Player (the built-in app) already plays SWF files with Ruffle's web build; in web pages, Chromium keeps the extension; - the frames extension (web pages inside the desktop's frames): not needed (the pages open in Chromium); - Chromium's policies and flags for the desktop (shortcuts, the camera, the GPU): WebKit's own settings, and the keyboard guard of #151 in the page itself; - the memory guard's "the largest web page": it closes Chromium's tabs, as now; the desktop itself is WebKit and is not one of them.

docs.t: System Settings › Desktop engine: a list, Standard (Chromium) or Lite (WebKit, test); the choice is kept in /persist/etc/rudolf-desktop-engine and taken by rudolf-init at start-up, so it applies at the next restart. Lite is rudolf-webkit (iso/sys/rudolf-webkit.c, WebKitGTK 4.1) in the system layer, with what it needs gathered by systools/addwebkit.sh from the release machine's Ubuntu 24.04 (its helper processes, GStreamer's basic plug-ins, GLib's TLS module): it starts before sign-in, with or without Debian and "Encrypt my data". (A first version used WebKitGTK in Debian, which with Debian in the encrypted folder, as on the Vivobook, could not start before sign-in.) Not yet: H.264 and AAC (GStreamer's libav plug-in, about 30 MB more). The workflow "Lite engine check" builds it and opens the desktop page in it on a virtual screen whenever its files change. Its first runs (WebKitGTK 2.52.6): the base layer grows from 197 to 232 MB (+34 MB to download once, +140 MB on the disk, 35 more libraries); the desktop page at the sign-in screen, drawn in software on the virtual screen, took 507 MB PSS (the page's process 379 MB, the window 93, the network 35). All 44 built-in apps opened in WebKit on the Vivobook without
