docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.7: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught › Added on 2026-11-10: safeguards against a computer that cannot start
docs.t: The Vivobook could not start the 1.5.7 beta with the Lite desktop engine, and Recovery mode, a boot-files-only rescue stick and a stick's updater each made it worse (the account is in docs/plan-1.5.8.md). Priorities 1 to 3 of the safeguards went into 1.5.7: a desktop that cannot start is given up (Lite on trial until it answers once), a system slot missing a layer goes back to the previous one, Recovery mode starts the installed system with safe settings, recovery and stick starts never update the installed system, and updates are self-contained and checked complete. Priorities 4 and 5 are docs/plan-1.5.8.md.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery
docs.t: Asked for on 2026-11-10, after the Vivobook could not start the 1.5.7 beta with the Lite desktop engine. The safeguards that stop such a failure from leaving a computer unable to start went into 1.5.7 (priorities 1 to 3 below); this plan is the rest (priorities 4 and 5). It starts once 1.5.7 is promoted. Added the same day: mobile data (Part 6, after looking at a Verizon MiFi 7730L), Android apps (Part 7: the .apk work delayed from 1.5.7, with workarounds) and mobile form factors (Part 8: x86 handhelds and tablets first, then a lean phone-capable Rudolf OS over the next versions) and Oracle's tabs in WebKit (Part 9: a real browser in the Lite desktop).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › What happened (2026-11-10)
docs.t: 1. Lite (WebKit) was chosen for the desktop. On the Vivobook's graphics it closed as it started, every 7 to 9 seconds; the session started it again without end, because its safety net only caught a desktop that hangs. The screen stayed grey and the computer never reached the sign-in screen. Lite had been tried on Xvfb and in Debian's own WebKit (cog), never on the Vivobook's real graphics.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › What happened (2026-11-10)
docs.t: 2. Recovery mode skipped the installed system for the drive's own, and an installed computer's drive has boot files only: "this drive has boot files only (1.2.8)". The rescue stick at hand had boot files only too, and both drives showed the same message, so it took three tries to see which drive had started. Fast Boot also skipped the stick until it was chosen in the ASUS boot menu.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › What happened (2026-11-10)
docs.t: 3. A full 1.5.6 stick (written with Rufus in DD mode from the Asus desktop) got through. Started in Recovery mode, it ran the stick's 1.5.6 with the Vivobook's 1.5.7 files: the desktop asked for the shell again and again and kept restarting. Its updater then put 1.5.7 in the spare slot taking the Chromium layer from the stick, and scheduled it; without the stick that slot could not start, and the start-up stopped at the same boot-files-only message (it went back to the good system at the following start only because the slot's tries had run out). chip then did not answer at start-up ("Codec #0 probe error", after the forced power-offs); a full shut-down fixed it. in /run, lost at each restart.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Done in 1.5.7 (priorities 1 to 3)
docs.t: A desktop that cannot start is given up (session: desk_exited, webkit_trial_*, shell_switch_limit; test qt/host/deskfall57_t.sh): Lite closing 3 times in a row as it starts, or not having answered before the computer was switched off, is turned off for good (Settings says when and why); the shell likewise until the next start; a desktop asking for the shell more than 3 times in 5 minutes is not obeyed. A system that cannot be put together goes back to the previous one (initramfs: a slot missing a layer is given up like a damaged one; test qt/host/startfall57_t.sh).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Done in 1.5.7 (priorities 1 to 3)
docs.t: Recovery mode starts the installed system with safe settings and changes nothing (initramfs; the session already leaves out Lite, the shell and the graphics driver in recovery). Needs 1.5.7 boot files. Recovery and stick starts never change the installed system (rudolf-update: no download in recovery, or from a disc that is not on RUDOLFDATA's drive; boot-ok does nothing in recovery; Settings says why; tests qt/host/updsafe57_t.sh and qt/shell2/updsafe57_t.js). Updates are self-contained and checked complete (rudolf-update: a layer shared with a removable disc is copied into the slot; a slot is only scheduled when every file is there at its listed size).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Priority 4: diagnosing a computer whose desktop does not start › 4.1 Start logs that outlast a restart
docs.t: Keep the session log, Lite's log (webkit-desktop.log), the start-up's choice of system (which slot, why, recovery or not) and the kernel's warnings of the last 4 starts in /persist/var/log/starts/ (rotated like rudolfd.log), written as they happen, not at shut-down. The initramfs writes its decisions (slot chosen, tries left, layer missing, slot given up) to RUDOLFDATA before kexec, so a start that never reaches rudolf-init still leaves a record. System health shows "Last starts" with the outcome of each; the self-test and Blitzen's diagnostics read them.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Priority 4: diagnosing a computer whose desktop does not start › 4.2 The devlink and remote access without the desktop
docs.t: starts it at boot when its time is left, and whether it waits for the desktop or the network the desktop sets up). independent of the desktop process, once the network is up. Remote access serves the X screen, so it shows a grey or broken desktop too: make sure it does not depend on the desktop page either.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Priority 4: diagnosing a computer whose desktop does not start › 4.3 Emergency keys in rudolf-display
docs.t: A key combination handled by rudolf-display itself (which reads the keyboard before X, as Ctrl+Alt+Del does) that switches the desktop back to the standard engine at once and restarts it: for example Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F12, with an on-screen line from rudolf-display saying it did. The same keys in Recovery mode do nothing (already safe).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Priority 5: smoother recovery and fewer surprises › 5.1 Rescue media that say what they are
docs.t: Make a stick writes a full rescue system by default; a boot-files-only stick stays possible but says so on its boot menu title and when it starts. Start-up messages name the drive they are about ("the USB stick SanDisk 64 GB" / "this computer's drive") and say what to do next. The "boot files only (1.2.8)" message drops the version (it is when the feature came, not the drive's version) and says whether a rescue stick was found.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Priority 5: smoother recovery and fewer surprises › 5.2 Help: starting from a stick
docs.t: A Help page: Fast Boot (ASUS and others) can skip USB sticks; use the one-time boot menu (Esc or F8 on ASUS, F12 on many others) or turn Fast Boot off; write sticks in DD mode; Windows then calls the stick "not accessible" (do not format it); choose Recovery mode in Rudolf OS's menu.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Priority 5: smoother recovery and fewer surprises › 5.3 A speaker chip that does not answer
docs.t: The self-test checks that every sound card's codec answered at start-up (the kernel's "no codecs initialized" / "Codec #N probe error"), and System health says "The sound chip did not answer at start-up: shut down fully (not restart), wait 10 seconds and turn the computer on". rudolf-init tries once to reset it (unbind and bind the HD Audio device) before the desktop starts.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Priority 5: smoother recovery and fewer surprises › 5.4 Test where the risk is
docs.t: A rule for the repository: anything that changes how the desktop starts (engine, shell, display) has its fallback tested first, on the real graphics path (Xorg with the GPU, in QEMU with virtio-gpu and on the Vivobook), not only on the software display; it reaches the Vivobook only after that. libGLESv2.so.2": WebKit opens it while running, so addwebkit.sh's ldd pass never saw it. Fixed in 1.5.7 (addwebkit.sh copies it; the self-test checks it; webkit-check.yml runs Lite from the base layer in a chroot). With it, Lite ran, but GTK could not use the GPU ("No available configurations for the given pixel format", Xorg with modesetting on AMD): WebKit draws in software. Left for 1.5.8: GPU drawing for Lite (GTK's GL on this X server), and its effect on memory and speed.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Staging toward 1.6.0, the first cellular release (added on 2026-11-10)
docs.t: Parts 6 to 8 are staged across three versions (docs/plan-1.5.9.md, docs/plan-1.6.0.md): 1.5.8 (this plan): Oracle's tabs in WebKit (Part 9); the network groundwork: 6.1 the kernel's USB modem drivers, 6.2 adapters plugged in after start-up, 6.3 metered connections; 7.1 the .apk wizard's information, 7.2 scrcpy, the kernel side of 7.3 (binder); 8.1 begun (the tablet layout in the desktop, with browser tests). 1.5.9: ModemManager (read only), the WWAN kernel subsystem and the operators' database; 8.1 finished (tablet mode, on-screen keyboard, rotation); 8.2 the ARM64 build with QEMU checks on a test channel; 6.4 Share this connection; 7.3 Waydroid in Debian; the first phone prepared.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Staging toward 1.6.0, the first cellular release (added on 2026-11-10)
docs.t: 1.6.0: cellular: SIM and PIN, APNs, connecting, priorities and failover, data limits, signal and status, SMS (Messages), airplane mode, the FCC unlock for laptop modules; the first ARM64 release. Voice and emergency calls, and phones themselves, in 1.6.x (8.3). 6.5 (a hotspot's own status) stays as written: Rudolf OS shows the connection, never signs in to the hotspot.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 6: mobile data (added on 2026-11-10)
docs.t: Looked at on 2026-11-10: a used Verizon Jetpack MiFi 7730L (Novatel/Inseego, January 2017) plugged into the Asus desktop. LTE Category 9 (3-carrier aggregation, 2x2 MIMO, nano SIM), Wi-Fi 802.11ac on 2.4 and 5 GHz at once (15 devices), a 4,400 mAh battery, a 2.4" 320x240 touchscreen, USB-C and USB-A, a Qualcomm modem (the chip is not published), and 128 MB of memory with 256 MB of storage. Rudolf OS cannot run on it: far too little memory and storage, and its firmware is signed and locked (no open firmware such as OpenWrt supports it). Its use is as the **cellular link of a Rudolf OS laptop or tablet**, over USB or Wi-Fi. On the Asus, Windows listed it as a device but not as a network adapter (USB tethering off in its menu, or no active SIM), so which USB protocol it uses is still to be seen.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 6: mobile data (added on 2026-11-10)
docs.t: What Rudolf OS lacks for that (checked in the code on 2026-11-10):

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 6: mobile data (added on 2026-11-10) › 6.1 USB modems and tethered phones
docs.t: The kernel has the USB CDC Ethernet driver (USB_NET_CDCETHER) only. Add USB_NET_RNDIS_HOST (many hotspots and Android phones' USB tethering), USB_NET_CDC_NCM and USB_NET_CDC_MBIM (newer hotspots and phones), USB_NET_QMI_WWAN and USB_SERIAL_OPTION (cellular modules inside laptops and USB sticks), checked in kconfig.sh like the others. ModemManager (with libqmi and libmbim) for cellular modules that need to be told to connect, with the SIM's PIN asked by the desktop: 1.5.9 (read only) and 1.6.0 (connecting); hotspots and tethered phones need none of it (they hand out an address themselves), so 1.5.8 covers them fully.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 6: mobile data (added on 2026-11-10) › 6.2 A network adapter plugged in after start-up
docs.t: rudolf-init asks for an address (udhcpc) only on cables present at start-up. An adapter that appears later (a hotspot's USB cable, a phone's tethering switched on, a USB Ethernet dongle) gets none: mdev runs the same DHCP start for a new network interface, and stops it when it goes. Settings › Network lists it ("USB modem: MiFi 7730L").

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 6: mobile data (added on 2026-11-10) › 6.3 Metered connections
docs.t: A connection can be metered (cellular data with a cap): set automatically for USB modems and tethered phones and for Wi-Fi networks that say so (Android's hotspots set the ANDROID_METERED option in DHCP), and by hand in Settings › Network for any network. On a metered connection: no automatic system updates (sysupd25's daily check downloads nothing; Settings says why and offers it by hand), no automatic Library, Flathub or Blitzen downloads, no app store catalog refresh in the background; the browser and apps work as usual. rudolfd keeps the state (net/metered), the desktop reads it. Data used on each metered connection this month (from the interface's counters), in Settings › Network.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 6: mobile data (added on 2026-11-10) › 6.4 Rudolf OS as the hotspot ("Share this connection") (1.5.9)
docs.t: The Vivobook's Wi-Fi chip (rtw88 8821CE) supports access-point mode. Settings › Network › Share this connection: shares the connection Rudolf OS has (cable, USB modem, or Wi-Fi on a second adapter) over Wi-Fi with its own network name and password (hostapd, dnsmasq, and the firewall's NAT rules), off by default, administrators only. With one Wi-Fi chip, sharing a Wi-Fi connection over the same chip depends on the chip (concurrent station and access point): checked on the Vivobook first, otherwise offered only for cable and USB connections.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 6: mobile data (added on 2026-11-10) › 6.5 Battery and signal of a hotspot
docs.t: Hotspots and phones expose little over USB: what Rudolf OS can show without signing in to the hotspot is the connection itself (speed, data used). A hotspot's own admin page stays the hotspot's (its address in Settings › Network, opened in Oracle); Rudolf OS does not sign in to it or keep its password.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 7: Android apps (.apk), delayed from 1.5.7, with workarounds (added on 2026-11-10)
docs.t: On 2026-11-10 .apk was moved out of 1.5.7: Waydroid needs the kernel's binder, Waydroid and its container tools in the system layer, and a first download of about 1 GB (the Android system image), which weighs on a 3.4 GB computer while the desktop is being made lighter. These are the ways to it, cheapest first; the .apk wizard (install56) offers what this computer can do.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 7: Android apps (.apk), delayed from 1.5.7, with workarounds (added on 2026-11-10) › 7.1 Always: say what the .apk is, and offer what already works
docs.t: Opening an .apk shows the app's name, icon, version and the permissions it asks for (read from the file with aapt2 dump badging, from Debian's Android tools, or a small reader of the APK's manifest in rudolfd), never running it. It offers what Rudolf OS already runs: the app's web version (many Android apps are also websites or web apps; Oracle can keep one as an app in the Start menu) and the same app for Linux (Flathub, by name, in the App Store), when there is one.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 7: Android apps (.apk), delayed from 1.5.7, with workarounds (added on 2026-11-10) › 7.2 The phone's own apps on Rudolf OS (scrcpy)
docs.t: An Android phone plugged in by USB (or on the same Wi-Fi) shows its screen in a Rudolf OS window and is used with the mouse and keyboard (with its sound on Android 11 or later): scrcpy (from Debian), over ADB. The apps run on the phone, so nothing is installed on the computer and nothing is downloaded beyond scrcpy (a few MB). It needs "USB debugging" turned on in the phone's developer options, by the phone's owner: Rudolf OS explains how and never changes anything on the phone itself. (Normal ADB only: not the diagnostic or download modes of a phone's chip, which can damage it.)

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 7: Android apps (.apk), delayed from 1.5.7, with workarounds (added on 2026-11-10) › 7.2 The phone's own apps on Rudolf OS (scrcpy)
docs.t: scrcpy works with Android 5 or later; the phones seen on the Asus (a REDMAGIC 9 Pro, a moto g play) are recent enough.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 7: Android apps (.apk), delayed from 1.5.7, with workarounds (added on 2026-11-10) › 7.3 Android apps on the computer (Waydroid), for computers with room for it
docs.t: The kernel side costs almost nothing and can ship first, in 1.5.8: ANDROID_BINDER_IPC, ANDROID_BINDERFS (and ANDROID_BINDER_DEVICES=""), with the namespaces and cgroups Waydroid's LXC container uses (most are on already), checked in kconfig.sh. Then Waydroid can be added later without a new kernel. Waydroid itself in Debian (already a download on demand), not in the system layer: apt install waydroid in Debian's container, with binderfs mounted into it, so the system layer does not grow and computers that never open an .apk pay nothing.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 7: Android apps (.apk), delayed from 1.5.7, with workarounds (added on 2026-11-10) › 7.3 Android apps on the computer (Waydroid), for computers with room for it
docs.t: The Android image (LineageOS, about 800 MB) only when the person asks, behind a confirmation with the size, kept in the encrypted folder's storage like Debian, and removable in Storage. Offered only on computers with at least 4 GB of memory, or with the Lite desktop engine on (it frees roughly 300 to 500 MB), and the memory guard treats Waydroid's container as an app it may close. Each Android app gets its own window (Waydroid's multi-window mode, its Wayland display shown inside X with a small compositor), and a Start menu entry.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 7: Android apps (.apk), delayed from 1.5.7, with workarounds (added on 2026-11-10) › 7.3 Android apps on the computer (Waydroid), for computers with room for it
docs.t: Apps that need Google's services (most from Google Play) may not work; the wizard says so before the download. Waydroid with OpenGApps or microG is left to the person (a setting in Waydroid, not something Rudolf OS installs).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 7: Android apps (.apk), delayed from 1.5.7, with workarounds (added on 2026-11-10) › 7.4 Lighter, experimental: Android Translation Layer
docs.t: The Android Translation Layer (used by postmarketOS) runs some simple Android apps as ordinary Linux programs, with no Android image at all. It runs few apps today; looked at again once 7.3 works, as a light option for the apps it runs.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 7: Android apps (.apk), delayed from 1.5.7, with workarounds (added on 2026-11-10) › 7.5 Rudolf OS on a phone
docs.t: The desktop's browser build (iso/www/index.html) already runs in any web browser, without rudolfd. On a phone it could be added to the home screen as a web app (a manifest and a service worker, so it opens offline and full screen), with the touch layout the desktop has for tablets: Notepad, WordPro, the games, Blitzen's packs and the files kept in the browser. Rudolf OS as a system on phone hardware (its own kernel on a phone) is not planned: phones' boot loaders are locked and their drivers closed.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 7: Android apps (.apk), delayed from 1.5.7, with workarounds (added on 2026-11-10) › 7.6 iPhone apps (.ipa)
docs.t: Unchanged from 1.5.6's plan: they cannot run outside Apple's devices; the wizard says so and looks for a web or Linux version.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 8: mobile form factors, and a phone-capable Rudolf OS (added on 2026-11-10)
docs.t: The aim: Rudolf OS on handhelds, tablets and, within the next few versions, phones, while staying lean (a phone has 4 to 8 GB of memory and runs on a battery). Two routes, the cheap one first.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 8: mobile form factors, and a phone-capable Rudolf OS (added on 2026-11-10) › What stands in the way today (checked in the code on 2026-11-10)
docs.t: x86 only: the release builds x86-64 layers, and x86 paths are written into ci_release.sh, addwebkit.sh, addnvk.sh and the self-test (/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu). Phones are ARM64. One kernel for every PC, started by UEFI (systemd-boot, a signed UKI, Secure Boot). Phones need a kernel and a device tree per model, started by the phone's own boot loader (Android boot images, or U-Boot on the PinePhone Pro). A desktop for a mouse and keyboard: touch works (rudolf-display reads touchscreens), but there is no on-screen keyboard, no portrait layout, no gestures, and windows are sized for a large screen. No phone services: no cellular modem handling, calls or SMS, no suspend that keeps the modem listening, no screen rotation from the sensors, no phone cameras.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 8: mobile form factors, and a phone-capable Rudolf OS (added on 2026-11-10) › What stands in the way today (checked in the code on 2026-11-10)
docs.t: Weight: the Chromium layer (about 130 MB compressed) and the standard engine's memory (about 830 MB on the Vivobook); Debian, Wine and Steam are already downloads on demand.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 8: mobile form factors, and a phone-capable Rudolf OS (added on 2026-11-10) › Leanness rules for every mobile step
docs.t: 1. Lite (WebKit) is the desktop engine on mobile devices, not Standard: about a third of Chromium's memory (the 1.5.7 trial). Chromium becomes a download on demand there, for websites that need it. 2. Nothing heavy in the system layer: Debian, Wine, Steam, Waydroid, Blitzen's model, scrcpy and the like stay downloads on demand, behind a confirmation with the size, removable in Storage.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 8: mobile form factors, and a phone-capable Rudolf OS (added on 2026-11-10) › Leanness rules for every mobile step
docs.t: 3. Measured on the device, against budgets: the system layers under 400 MB compressed; the desktop at the sign-in screen under 400 MB of memory with Lite (about 520 MB in the release check on 2026-11-10: WebKit's web process 389 MB, its UI 94 MB, its network process 35 MB, on Xvfb; reducing it is part of 8.2); idle power measured over an hour with the screen off. A release that breaks a budget says so in the release check, like the Lite engine check. 4. The same release, one system per architecture: one version number and one CHANGELOG; the desktop (the web page) is identical everywhere; only the layers below it differ.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 8: mobile form factors, and a phone-capable Rudolf OS (added on 2026-11-10) › 8.1 x86 handhelds and tablets (1.5.8 to 1.5.9): no port needed
docs.t: Target devices: Steam Deck, ASUS ROG Ally, Lenovo Legion Go, Microsoft Surface Go and other x86 tablets. They start Rudolf OS as it is (UEFI, x86-64); Secure Boot as on any PC. Touch layout (the desktop): a tablet mode chosen automatically when there is a touchscreen and no keyboard (and by hand in Settings › Display): bigger targets, the taskbar as a dock, windows full screen one at a time, swipe from the bottom for the Start menu and from the right for notifications, portrait and landscape.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 8: mobile form factors, and a phone-capable Rudolf OS (added on 2026-11-10) › 8.1 x86 handhelds and tablets (1.5.8 to 1.5.9): no port needed
docs.t: On-screen keyboard: part of the desktop page (it is a web page, so its own keyboard works in every built-in app and in Oracle's pages); for X programs (Linux and Windows apps), rudolf-display types its keys through XTest as it types the hardware keyboard's. Rotation from the accelerometer (iio-sensor-proxy, or reading /sys/bus/iio directly) through rudolf-display, which already rotates and scales the screen. Mobile data (Part 6) and battery care (1.4.4 on) apply as they are. Tests: browser tests at tablet and phone sizes (portrait 1080x2340 scaled, touch events); QEMU x86 with a touchscreen (-device virtio-tablet / usb-tablet with multitouch) and a portrait screen; then the Vivobook with the

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 8: mobile form factors, and a phone-capable Rudolf OS (added on 2026-11-10) › 8.2 The ARM64 build (built and checked in QEMU in 1.5.9; first released in 1.6.0): Rudolf OS on ARM
docs.t: Build: the release workflow builds a second set of layers on GitHub's ARM64 runners (ubuntu-24.04-arm): the base layer, Lite (WebKitGTK for arm64), rudolfd and the C helpers (they are portable C), and the desktop page unchanged. The x86 paths become $(gcc -print-multiarch); addwebkit.sh and the self-test take the architecture from the system. Not on ARM64 at first: Steam and Windows programs (x86 only; Box64 or FEX as a later download, measured first), the NVIDIA (nvk) layer, Flash's Ruffle stays (it is WebAssembly). Updates: the same signed manifest format, with a list per architecture (beta/arm64/manifest.txt); the updater takes its architecture's list and never another's.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 8: mobile form factors, and a phone-capable Rudolf OS (added on 2026-11-10) › 8.2 The ARM64 build (built and checked in QEMU in 1.5.9; first released in 1.6.0): Rudolf OS on ARM
docs.t: QEMU checks (what QEMU can confirm): qemu-system-aarch64 -M virt with UEFI (edk2), virtio-gpu, a virtio touchscreen, 3 to 4 GB of memory and a portrait screen: the system starts, the desktop runs in Lite, updates and rollback work, Recovery mode and the safeguards work, and a USB modem passed through to the virtual machine (the MiFi 7730L) gets an address. What QEMU cannot confirm: a phone's display, GPU, modem, cameras, sensors and audio drivers, its sleep and wake, battery life and heat, and how its boot loader starts the kernel. Those need the phone.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 8: mobile form factors, and a phone-capable Rudolf OS (added on 2026-11-10) › 8.2 The ARM64 build (built and checked in QEMU in 1.5.9; first released in 1.6.0): Rudolf OS on ARM
docs.t: Generic ARM64 computers first: ARM64 laptops and boards that start with UEFI (Snapdragon X laptops as their mainline support matures; the Raspberry Pi 5 with its UEFI firmware) run the same image as QEMU.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 8: mobile form factors, and a phone-capable Rudolf OS (added on 2026-11-10) › 8.3 Phones (1.6.x): one well-supported phone first
docs.t: Candidates (boot loader unlockable, good mainline Linux support; checked against the postmarketOS device list when the work starts): PinePhone Pro (made for Linux; the easiest to work on, slow), OnePlus 6/6T (Snapdragon 845, long among the best-supported Android phones on mainline Linux; cheap used), **Google Pixel 3a or a newer Pixel bought unlocked from Google (not one sold by Verizon), Fairphone 4/5** (the maker supports unlocking and Linux ports), Purism Librem 5 (Linux-first, expensive). The test phones at hand are not suitable: the moto g play XT2093DL is a carrier prepaid model, normally not unlockable; whether the REDMAGIC 9 Pro's boot loader unlocks is to be checked before relying on it. Only a phone that may be experimented on.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 8: mobile form factors, and a phone-capable Rudolf OS (added on 2026-11-10) › 8.3 Phones (1.6.x): one well-supported phone first
docs.t: Per-phone kernel, shared everything else: a device package per phone (its kernel config fragment, device tree, firmware list, boot image format), built from postmarketOS's mainline work where it exists (their kernel configs and patches are the reference); the base, Lite and desktop layers are the ARM64 build's.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 8: mobile form factors, and a phone-capable Rudolf OS (added on 2026-11-10) › 8.3 Phones (1.6.x): one well-supported phone first
docs.t: Starting and updating: the phone's boot loader starts a Rudolf OS boot image (kernel, device tree, the same initramfs) from the boot partition; the A/B system slots, the signed manifest, rollback and the safeguards are the same as on a PC, kept on the userdata partition as RUDOLFDATA. Installing: from a computer, with fastboot (a guided page in Rudolf OS on the PC, and the steps in Help); the phone's boot loader stays unlocked, so it has no Secure Boot: the dm-verity check of each layer against the signed list still runs, and Settings says plainly that the phone's boot loader is unlocked.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 8: mobile form factors, and a phone-capable Rudolf OS (added on 2026-11-10) › 8.3 Phones (1.6.x): one well-supported phone first
docs.t: Phone services, each a small part: the cellular modem and mobile data (ModemManager, Part 6), SMS and calls (ModemManager's messaging and voice, with a Phone and a Messages app in the desktop; emergency calls only once tested on that phone), suspend with the modem able to wake the phone (calls, messages), screen rotation and the proximity sensor (iio), the cameras (libcamera, where the phone's are supported), audio routing for calls (ALSA's UCM files from the phone's port). The phone shell: the tablet layout of 8.1 at phone size: one app at a time, the Start menu as an app grid, a status bar (signal, battery, time), a lock screen with notifications, the on-screen keyboard.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 8: mobile form factors, and a phone-capable Rudolf OS (added on 2026-11-10) › 8.3 Phones (1.6.x): one well-supported phone first
docs.t: Phone budgets: the desktop with Lite under 400 MB at the sign-in screen; the system layers for a phone under 400 MB compressed; idle drain with the screen off and the modem on measured over a night, compared with postmarketOS on the same phone.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 8: mobile form factors, and a phone-capable Rudolf OS (added on 2026-11-10) › 8.4 Before any of it is offered
docs.t: The testing rule (docs/testing.md) applies: the fallback first (on a phone: the previous slot, Recovery mode from the boot menu, the safe desktop), tests from the built system, the real hardware path, and the device last with its Each step ships as a test first (as Lite did), and only to devices that pass the release check for their architecture.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 9: Oracle's tabs in WebKit (added on 2026-11-10)
docs.t: On the Vivobook with Lite (beta 2026111100, 2026-11-10), Oracle sent every website to Chromium's own window (the design of 1.5.7's Lite: the desktop page cannot show most sites in its frames, which sites forbid), and that window went behind the desktop at once, so browsing looked broken. With Standard, Oracle's tabs are real Chromium pages (the shell). Lite gets the same: Oracle's tabs as real WebKit pages.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 9: Oracle's tabs in WebKit (added on 2026-11-10) › 9.1 How
docs.t: rudolf-webkit (WebKitGTK, our own program) makes a web view per Oracle tab, laid over the desktop page exactly where Oracle draws its page area (a GtkOverlay above the desktop's view), shown, hidden, moved and closed as the page asks. A native view is not a frame: sites' frame protections do not apply, and sign-ins work as in a browser. The page and rudolf-webkit talk through a WebKit script message handler (page to program: open, navigate, back, forward, reload, stop, close, show, hide, place, zoom, find) and a script run in the page (program to page: address, title, icon, loading progress, security state, can-go-back, new tab or window wanted, download started).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 9: Oracle's tabs in WebKit (added on 2026-11-10) › 9.1 How
docs.t: Websites' data apart from the desktop's: their own WebKitWebsiteDataManager in ~/.rudolf-webkit/web, with cookies kept; private tabs with an ephemeral one; Settings › Oracle's clear-data buttons act on it. Popups and sign-in windows become new tabs (or a small window for window.open with a size, as sign-in popups need, with window.opener working so the sign-in returns to the page). Downloads through WebKitDownload into Downloads, shown in Oracle's downloads and the notifications, as dl27 does for Chromium's. Permissions (camera, microphone, location, notifications) asked through the desktop's own prompt, per site, remembered as Oracle's site settings. Fullscreen video: the tab's view fills the screen; Esc leaves.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 9: Oracle's tabs in WebKit (added on 2026-11-10) › 9.1 How
docs.t: Keyboard and focus: the tab's view has the focus when clicked; the desktop's shortcuts still work (rudolf-display and the program pass them to the page). Flash: Ruffle injected as a user script in the tabs (it is JavaScript and WebAssembly). Input from other windows: Task Manager, notifications and menus drawn by the desktop page stay above the tab views (the program hides or clips a view under them, as the shell does).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 9: Oracle's tabs in WebKit (added on 2026-11-10) › 9.2 What stays Chromium's
docs.t: Sites that need Widevine (Netflix, Spotify, Disney+), H.264/AAC where no other format is offered, Chrome-only sites and Chrome extensions: Oracle offers "Open in Chromium" (a button in the address bar and in the page's menu), and opens such sites there by itself when a site is on the list or a playback fails for want of a codec; the browser window comes to the front and stays there (the 1.5.7 bug fixed first, below). YouTube plays in WebKit through its VP9/AV1 and Opus streams.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 9: Oracle's tabs in WebKit (added on 2026-11-10) › 9.3 Leanness
docs.t: Each tab is a WebKit web process (about the size of a Chromium tab), with no second browser running at all unless a site needs Chromium; hidden tabs can be suspended (WebKit's page freezing), and the memory guard treats tab views as pages it may end, as it does Chromium's. No new layer: WebKitGTK is already in the system (1.5.7).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 9: Oracle's tabs in WebKit (added on 2026-11-10) › 9.4 First, in 1.5.7
docs.t: The browser window comes to the front when Oracle opens a site in Lite, and stays there until the person goes back to the desktop (the desktop page and rudolf-display no longer bring the desktop back over it).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 9: Oracle's tabs in WebKit (added on 2026-11-10) › 9.6 FedCM on or off, in Oracle's ☰ menu (added on 2026-11-10)
docs.t: On the Vivobook, "Sign in with Google" on claude.ai went through Chromium's FedCM and stopped on a blank accounts.google.com/gsi/transform window; Firefox, without FedCM, signed in. 1.5.7 turns FedCM off in Chromium for everyone (PR #198). It is a choice, since some sites may come to need FedCM and Google may change its sign-in again: Oracle's ☰ menu: "Sign-in with FedCM" with a tick (off by default), and the same switch in Settings › Oracle › Sign-in, with one line on what it does ("Sites' 'Sign in with Google' buttons use Chromium's own sign-in. Turn it on only if a site asks for it; with it, Google's sign-in stopped on a blank window on some computers").

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 9: Oracle's tabs in WebKit (added on 2026-11-10) › 9.6 FedCM on or off, in Oracle's ☰ menu (added on 2026-11-10)
docs.t: Where it is kept: a system setting, /persist/etc/rudolf-browser.conf (fedcm=0|1), since Chromium's flags are set for the whole browser, not per account; rudolfd GET/POST web/fedcm (any signed-in account may change it, as other browser settings; guests cannot). The desktop page reads it at start-up for the menu's tick. What it changes: rudolfd web/open leaves FedCm out of --disable-features when on; the session reads the file when it starts the desktop's Chromium (Oracle's real tabs with Standard).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 9: Oracle's tabs in WebKit (added on 2026-11-10) › 9.6 FedCM on or off, in Oracle's ☰ menu (added on 2026-11-10)
docs.t: When it applies: the browser window is restarted at once if it is open (after asking: "Close the browser window to apply? Its tabs come back"; Chromium restores them); real tabs need the desktop's Chromium restarted, so the menu says "Applies to Oracle's tabs at the next sign-in or restart" and offers "Restart Oracle's tabs now" (the shell's restart, which keeps the session). Lite's WebKit tabs (9.1): WebKitGTK has no FedCM; the menu item is shown greyed with "Not used by WebKit tabs" while the tab is a WebKit one, and still applies to sites sent to Chromium (9.2).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 9: Oracle's tabs in WebKit (added on 2026-11-10) › 9.6 FedCM on or off, in Oracle's ☰ menu (added on 2026-11-10)
docs.t: If a sign-in stops on a blank accounts.google.com/gsi/... page (the address is known), Oracle's bar offers "Sign-in stuck? Try with FedCM off / on" once, switching the setting and reloading the sign-in.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Part 9: Oracle's tabs in WebKit (added on 2026-11-10) › 9.5 Tests
docs.t: rudolf-webkit's tab protocol: a host test that runs it on Xvfb with a local test site (frame-protected pages, a sign-in popup with window.opener, a download, a permission request, fullscreen), in the Lite engine check from the base layer (chroot) as for the desktop. Browser tests of Oracle's side with the program's messages stood in. FedCM switch: a host test that web/open and the session put FedCm in --disable-features exactly when the setting is off; a browser test of the ☰ menu tick, Settings › Oracle and the stuck-sign-in bar (stood-in rudolfd). fullscreen, memory with 5 tabs against Chromium's.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Steps
docs.t: 1. 4.1 start logs (initramfs, rudolf-init, session), with a host test of the rotation. Done (branch v158-startlogs): initramfs note/keeplog (var/log/boot-decisions.log, last 300 lines, kept before every hand-over, restart and stop; /etc/rudolf/initramfs.log), rudolf-init starts_keep (var/log/starts/0..3: start.txt, session's desk_up_mark, /usr/lib/rudolf/starts (JSON), rudolfd GET system/starts, System health › Last starts, and Blitzen's facts (the start before, the start-up's decisions). Tests: qt/host/startlogs58_t.sh, qt/shell2/starts58_t.js. To merge once 1.5.7 is promoted.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Steps
docs.t: 3. 4.3 emergency keys in rudolf-display; host test of the key handling. Done (branch v158-startlogs): Ctrl+Alt+Backspace held for a second runs /usr/lib/rudolf/desktop-safe (standard engine, no shell, desktop started again; Lite off for good with the reason); Help and Settings › Desktop engine mention it. Test qt/host/desksafe58_t.sh. (No on-screen line from rudolf-display: with Xorg on the GPU it cannot draw over the screen; the desktop coming back and System health say it.)

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Steps
docs.t: 4. 5.3 sound chip check and reset; 5.1 rescue media and messages; 5.2 Help page. 5.3 done (branch v158-startlogs): sound codec-check (run by rudolf-init 12 s after start-up) resets an HD Audio chip that did not answer, once, and says so in System health (hardware); the self-test's sound-chip check names one still silent with what to do. Test qt/host/codec58_t.sh. 5.2 done: Help › Starting from a USB stick (rescue). 5.1 in part: the boot-files-only message names the drive (USB stick or this computer's drive, with its model) and says what to do; Make a stick writing a full system by default is left. done: docs/testing.md. The Lite cause was found and fixed in 1.5.7 (libGLESv2); GPU drawing for Lite remains.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Steps
docs.t: 6. Part 6, mobile data: 6.1 kernel drivers (kconfig.sh) and 6.2 adapters plugged in later (mdev, udhcpc), with host tests; then 6.3 metered connections (rudolfd net/metered, sysupd25, lib52, the download wizards), with browser tests. The MiFi 7730L is tried once USB tethering is on (which driver it needs). (6.4 moves to 1.5.9.) 7. Part 7, Android apps: 7.1 the .apk wizard's information and alternatives; 7.2 scrcpy (needs only Debian); the kernel side of 7.3 (binder) in the same release; 7.5 the browser build as a phone web app. (Waydroid in Debian: 1.5.9.)

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.8: diagnosing a computer that does not start, and smoother recovery › Steps
docs.t: 8. Part 8, mobile form factors: in 1.5.8, 8.1's tablet layout in the desktop with browser tests (the on-screen keyboard, rotation and the QEMU and Vivobook checks finish it in 1.5.9); 8.2 the ARM64 build in 1.5.9, first released in 1.6.0; 8.3 one phone in 1.6.x (a PinePhone Pro or a OnePlus 6/6T), then the phone services one at a time; every step measured against the leanness budgets. 9. Part 9, Oracle's tabs in WebKit: 9.4 in 1.5.7 first; then the tab protocol in rudolf-webkit and Oracle's side (9.1), "Open in Chromium" (9.2), with the tests of 9.5; on the Vivobook last.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices
docs.t: Asked for on 2026-11-10, with docs/plan-1.6.0.md (the first cellular release): what 1.6.0 needs, staged between 1.5.8 and 1.5.9. 1.5.8 lays the network groundwork (docs/plan-1.5.8.md Part 6: USB modems' drivers, adapters plugged in later, metered connections); 1.5.9 adds the modem service, the tablet layout and the ARM64 build; 1.6.0 builds the cellular experience on them. It starts once 1.5.8 is promoted.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › From 1.5.8 (expected done there)
docs.t: Kernel drivers for USB networking from hotspots and phones (RNDIS, CDC-NCM, CDC-MBIM) and for cellular modules (QMI WWAN, the option serial driver), as modules. A network adapter plugged in after start-up gets an address; Settings › Network lists it. Metered connections, and what pauses on them. The kernel's Android binder (for Waydroid later), scrcpy, the .apk wizard's information.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 1: the modem service
docs.t: ModemManager (with libqmi, libmbim and libqrtr) in the system layer, started by mdev when a modem appears (a wwan* or cdc-wdm* device, or a USB modem's serial ports), stopped when the last one goes; D-Bus on the system bus (dbus-daemon already runs for the desktop session's needs). rudolfd mobile/status: modems (maker, model, firmware, driver), their SIM (present, locked, operator), state (registered, connected), signal, network type: read only in 1.5.9, shown in Settings › Network for each modem. No connecting yet: that is 1.6.0, once SIM, APN and metering are designed together. The operators' database (mobile-broadband-provider-info) in the system layer, for 1.6.0's APNs. Kernel: the WWAN subsystem (WWAN, MHI_WWAN_CTRL, MHI_WWAN_MBIM, IOSM for Intel's newer M.2 modems), as modules, checked in kconfig.sh.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 1: the modem service
docs.t: Budget: ModemManager and its libraries under 10 MB in the base layer (release check); nothing running without a modem. Tests: host tests with a stand-in ModemManager on a private D-Bus (rudolfd's parsing); the USB stick (1.6.0's test

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 2: tablet mode and the on-screen keyboard (docs/plan-1.5.8.md 8.1, finished)
docs.t: Tablet mode: chosen when there is a touchscreen and no keyboard, or by hand; dock, one window at a time, swipes. The on-screen keyboard: in the desktop page for its own apps and Oracle's pages; through rudolf-display (XTest) for Linux and Windows apps; it appears when a text field gets focus in tablet mode. Rotation from the accelerometer, through rudolf-display. Tests: browser tests at tablet and phone sizes with touch events; QEMU x86 with a touchscreen and a portrait screen; the Vivobook with tablet mode forced.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.5.9: the groundwork for cellular (1.6.0) and for mobile devices › Part 3: the ARM64 build (docs/plan-1.5.8.md 8.2)
docs.t: The release workflow builds ARM64 layers on GitHub's ARM64 runners, beside the x86 ones: base, Lite, rudolfd and the C helpers, the desktop page unchanged. The x86 library paths become the build machine's multiarch name. Not published yet: a test channel (beta-arm64/) used only by the QEMU checks. QEMU aarch64 checks in the release workflow (UEFI, virtio-gpu, a virtio touchscreen, 3 GB of memory, portrait): the system starts, the Lite desktop reaches the sign-in screen, an update installs and rolls back, Recovery mode and the safe desktop work. Not on ARM64: Steam, Windows programs, the nvk layer (see docs/plan-1.5.8.md 8.2).

docs.t: Rudolf OS as the hotspot: hostapd and dnsmasq in the system layer (about 1 MB), the firewall's NAT rules, off by with a Wi-Fi connection at the same time).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release
docs.t: Asked for on 2026-11-10: plan the first release of Rudolf OS that works with cellular networks, and stage what it needs in 1.5.8 and 1.5.9. It follows the mobile work in docs/plan-1.5.8.md (Parts 6 to 8) and docs/plan-1.5.9.md.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › What "cellular" means in 1.6.0
docs.t: Mobile data, by every common route, on x86 computers: a hotspot or phone on Wi-Fi (works today), a hotspot or phone over USB (1.5.8), a USB cellular stick, and a cellular module built into a laptop or tablet (M.2 WWAN cards: Quectel, Fibocom, Sierra Wireless, Telit). The SIM and the network handled in Rudolf OS: the SIM's PIN (and PUK), the operator's settings (APN) found by themselves, roaming on or off, signal, operator and network type in the taskbar, airplane mode. Living with a data plan: metered connections (1.5.8), data used this month and a limit, Wi-Fi preferred over cellular, and cellular as the fallback when Wi-Fi drops.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › What "cellular" means in 1.6.0
docs.t: Text messages, read and sent through the modem (carrier messages, sign-in codes), in a Messages app. ARM64: the first ARM64 release, for computers that start with UEFI (and QEMU), with the same cellular support. Not in 1.6.0: voice calls and emergency calls (a computer is not a phone, and emergency calling must be tested on each device before it is offered: 1.6.x, with the first phone), phones themselves (1.6.x, docs/plan-1.5.8.md 8.3), eSIM provisioning (downloading a carrier's eSIM profile), and 5G standalone features beyond what the modem does by itself.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Leanness
docs.t: Cellular support adds about 6 to 10 MB to the base layer (ModemManager, libqmi, libmbim, libqrtr, the operators' database, the kernel drivers as modules): measured in the release check against a 15 MB budget. ModemManager starts only when a modem is present (mdev starts it on the first modem it sees), so a computer without one runs nothing more. The Messages app is part of the desktop page (no new engine), and keeps messages in the account's folder.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 1. Modems (needs 1.5.9's ModemManager)
docs.t: ModemManager, with QMI, MBIM, QRTR and AT support, in the system layer; its D-Bus API read by rudolfd (mobile/*). FCC unlock: many laptop modules (Lenovo's and Dell's Fibocom and Quectel cards) start with their radio locked until the computer unlocks them. ModemManager's unlock scripts ship but are off; Settings offers "Turn on this laptop's cellular module" for the modules that need it, saying what it does, administrators only. Modules that Linux supports only partly (Intel's XMM7360 in some ThinkPads) are named in Settings with what is known about them, rather than failing silently.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 2. SIM and network (Settings › Mobile network)
docs.t: The SIM: present or not, locked with a PIN (asked once, by an administrator; three tries; the PUK after that, with the warning that a wrong PUK blocks the SIM for good), and the operator. The operator's settings (APN) from mobile-broadband-provider-info, by the SIM's operator code; a custom APN by hand. Roaming: off by default, with what it may cost. Preferred network type (5G, 4G, 3G) where the modem lets it be chosen. Airplane mode in the taskbar's quick settings: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and the modem off together (rfkill and ModemManager), and back as they were.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 3. The connection
docs.t: Connect and disconnect from the taskbar; connect automatically (on by default for the SIM's home network). Priority: cable, then Wi-Fi, then cellular; cellular stays connected but unused while Wi-Fi works, and carries the traffic within seconds when Wi-Fi drops (the routes' metrics), with a notification. The firewall applies to the cellular interface as to every other. IPv6 and IPv4 as the operator gives them (many operators are IPv6-only with NAT64/464XLAT: clat where needed).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 4. Data and money
docs.t: Metered by default on cellular (1.5.8's metered connections). Data used this month on each SIM, from the interface counters, kept across restarts; a monthly limit with a warning at 80 % and, if chosen, cellular data off at 100 %; the month's start day set by the person. Updates on cellular: never automatic; offered with the download size ("Download over mobile data: 42 MB").

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 5. Signal and status
docs.t: The taskbar shows signal bars, the network type (5G, LTE, 3G) and the operator, from ModemManager; Settings shows the signal's details (RSRP, RSRQ, SINR) for placing the computer or an antenna. System health: modem events (SIM removed, PIN blocked, no network, the module restarted). The self-test: the modem found, its driver, the SIM, registration, a data connection.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 6. Messages (SMS)
docs.t: A Messages app: conversations, read and send, delivery reports, notifications for new messages (also with the desktop locked: the sender and "new message", not the text, unless the person allows it). Messages kept in the account's folder (.rudolf/messages), and in the encrypted folder when "Encrypt my data" is on. Long messages and Unicode (multi-part SMS); MMS is left out (it needs the operator's MMS gateway and a separate APN).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Parts › 7. ARM64 (from 1.5.9's build)
docs.t: The first published ARM64 release: its own update list (beta/arm64/, stable/arm64/), a disc image for UEFI ARM64 computers, and the same parts 1 to 6. Proven in QEMU aarch64 and on one ARM64 computer before it is published.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Hardware to test with
docs.t: The MiFi 7730L (USB tethering and Wi-Fi), with an active SIM (or a prepaid data SIM). A USB cellular stick with an MBIM or QMI modem (for example a Quectel EC25 or EG25-G in a USB adapter: the same family as the PinePhone's modem, useful again in 1.6.x). A laptop with a WWAN module, or an M.2 WWAN card in an adapter: the Vivobook has no WWAN slot; a used ThinkPad with a Fibocom L850-GL or Quectel EM05-G card covers the FCC-unlock path. QEMU with the USB modems passed through (x86 and aarch64), for automated checks of everything above the radio.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Release checks for 1.6.0
docs.t: Host tests for each script and helper (ModemManager answers from a stand-in D-Bus service: SIM locked, PIN accepted, roaming, signal changes, a modem that disappears). Browser tests for Settings › Mobile network, the taskbar's signal, Messages, and the data limit. QEMU with a passed-through modem: connect, fail over from Wi-Fi (a virtual Wi-Fi link taken down) and back, data counted, the firewall on the cellular interface. modem is unplugged and plugged in again. The leanness budgets (docs/plan-1.5.8.md Part 8) and the cellular budget (15 MB) in the release check.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 1.6.0: the first cellular release › Steps
docs.t: 1. Parts 1 and 2 on the USB stick and the MiFi (1.5.9's ModemManager): modem found, SIM PIN, APN, connect. 2. Part 3 (priorities and failover) and part 4 (data and money). 3. Part 5 (signal and status) and the self-test. 4. Part 6 (Messages). 5. The FCC-unlock path on a laptop module. 6. Part 7: the ARM64 release with all of the above, after QEMU aarch64 and one ARM64 computer. 7. Betas on the Vivobook (with the USB stick and the MiFi) and the test laptop; promoted when the release checks pass.

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2)
docs.t: Apps made for Rudolf OS that not everyone needs move out of the system into an online catalog, from which the App Store downloads them, like Flathub for Linux apps. Apps made for Rudolf OS later go there too.

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › What moves, what stays
docs.t: | | Size (uncompressed) | 1.5.2 | |---|---|---| | Quake (LibreQuake data and the engine's source) | 27 MB | Library | | Emu (Nintendo DS and SNES emulators: DeSmuME, LakeSnes) | 2.6 MB | Library | | The desktop and its built-in apps (WOS Galaxy Map among them) | 4.4 MB | stays | | PDF viewer (pdf.js) | 3 MB | stays | | Japanese input dictionary | 5.2 MB | stays | | Luau | 4.1 MB | stays |

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › What moves, what stays
docs.t: The desktop layer gets about 30 MB smaller uncompressed (roughly half; about 12 MB less to download with every desktop update). Sober is not part of Rudolf OS: it is a Flatpak from Flathub, installed from the Games tab, and stays there. Only the large data and engines move. The few kilobytes of each app's own desktop code stay, so Quake and Emu stay in the Start menu and the Games tab; opened without their package, they offer to download it.

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › How it works: rpk, which Rudolf OS already has
docs.t: rpk (iso/sys/rpk.c) is Rudolf OS's package manager since 1.3.0: a package is a read-only squashfs image with an Ed25519 signature; installed packages are mounted at /pkg/<name>, so installing never changes the system and removing one deletes one file; kinds: webapp (www/ served by rudolfd at /pkg/<name>/, opened in a desktop window), addon (files the desktop uses), app, cli; a repository is static files: index.txt (one package per line) and index.sig, plus the packages; sources: the disc's own repository and lines in /persist/pkg/sources. The Library is an rpk repository on the internet, added to every computer's sources. Packages: rudolf-quake (addon): the files now in www/rudolfq, served at /pkg/rudolf-quake/www/; rudolf-emu (addon): the emulators now in www/lib/emu.

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › How it works: rpk, which Rudolf OS already has
docs.t: The desktop looks for them at /pkg/<name>/ instead of in its own folder.

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › Where it lives: a GitHub repository, yes, a separate one
docs.t: A GitHub repository is the right home, and a separate one, merciless146/rudolfos-library, is better than a folder in RudolfOS. Why GitHub: Hosting at no cost, and no server to run. The packages go in GitHub Releases (files up to 2 GB each), and the signed index in GitHub Pages. Rudolf OS's own updates already work this way, so nothing new needs to be learned or paid for. The host does not need to be trusted. rpk checks every package's signature against keys built into Rudolf OS, so a database server or anything more would add nothing. A build workflow (Actions) packs, signs and publishes each app, and keeps the history of every version. Why separate from RudolfOS:

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › Where it lives: a GitHub repository, yes, a separate one
docs.t: Its own schedule. A new version of an app is published by itself, without a Rudolf OS release, and every computer gets it through the App Store's updates. Its own key. See below: if the Library's key were ever stolen, it could not sign a system update. Room for others. People who make apps for Rudolf OS can later be given access to the Library repository without any access to the operating system or its keys. A clean RudolfOS repository, whose gh-pages branch holds only the system's update channels.

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › Where it lives: a GitHub repository, yes, a separate one
docs.t: Layout of rudolfos-library: ` apps/<name>/PKGINFO name, version, kind, title, description, icon, licence, category apps/<name>/www/... the app's files (or a fetch script for large data, pinned by SHA-256) .github/workflows/publish.yml build each changed app, sign it, upload it to a release, update the signed index ` Published: https://merciless146.github.io/rudolfos-library/index.txt, index.sig and catalog.json (titles, icons, descriptions, sizes, for the App Store), with the packages next to them (<name>.rpk). (As built: rpk takes each package's file from the same place as the list, so the packages are on Pages too, not in Releases.)

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › Keys: the Library gets its own
docs.t: Today /etc/rudolf/rpk-keys is trusted by both rpk (packages) and rudolf-update (the system's updates). A key added there for the Library could also sign a system update. So: a new Ed25519 key pair for the Library, made by you with the existing tool (as the release key was); its public key in a new file, /etc/rudolf/library-keys, which rpk trusts and rudolf-update does not. The release key keeps signing system updates only.

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › The App Store and the desktop
docs.t: A Rudolf OS Library tab in the App Store: each app with its icon, size, description and licence, and Get / Open / Remove / Update. Opening Quake or Emu without the package: "Quake is in the Rudolf OS Library (13 MB). Download it?", and it opens when the download finishes. Nobody loses an app: on the first start of 1.5.2, a computer whose Games folder or saves show it used Quake or Emu gets that package installed by itself (in the background, when online), with a notification.

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › The App Store and the desktop
docs.t: Offline: the disc image's own repository carries both packages, so an install from the disc or a live session can add them without internet. The download of the system shrinks, and the disc stays the same size. Updates: the App Store's Updates also checks the Library; the health log records installs and updates.

docs.t: 2. rudolfos-library: the layout, the publish workflow, the two packages; first publish. 3. Rudolf OS 1.5.2: - /etc/rudolf/library-keys, rpk trusting it, and the Library added to sources; - Quake and Emu reading their files from /pkg/; - the Library tab; - "download it?" when an app is missing; - reinstalling for computers that used them; - the disc repository carrying both packages; - www/rudolfq and www/lib/emu removed from the desktop layer. 4. Tests: - in the browser: the Library tab, download prompts, reinstall on update; - in QEMU: install from the Library over the network and from the disc, Quake and Emu running from /pkg/, removal; - a system update signed with the Library key is refused.

docs.h: Secure Boot
docs.t: Rudolf OS 1.2.2 starts on UEFI computers with Secure Boot on. This page says how, and what to do when a part of it has to change.

docs.h: Secure Boot › The chain
docs.t: | Step | File on the disc's UEFI image | Checked by | Signed with | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI, shim (Ubuntu's shim-signed) | the firmware (Microsoft's UEFI CA, in every PC) | Microsoft | | 2 | EFI/BOOT/grubx64.efi, systemd-boot: the boot menu | shim: the key enrolled in its key list (MOK) | the Rudolf OS key | | 3 | EFI/rudolf/rudolf.efi, the kernel bundle: systemd's stub, the kernel with its initramfs, fixed options | shim, through systemd-boot | the Rudolf OS key | | 4 | the system layers (RUDOLF/*.SFS) | dm-verity, against the root hashes in the signed release list RUDOLF/MANIFEST.TXT | the release key (Ed25519) | | 5 | an updated kernel in a slot on RUDOLFDATA (kexec) | the running kernel: the Rudolf OS certificate is built in as trusted | the Rudolf OS key |

docs.h: Secure Boot › The chain
docs.t: MokManager (EFI/BOOT/mmx64.efi) is where a person enrolls the Rudolf OS key the first time (EFI/rudolf/rudolf.cer), or confirms the request made by Settings > Security Settings > Prepare Secure Boot (rudolfd: POST /api/secureboot/prepare, MokNew and MokAuth with a one-time password). With Secure Boot on, the initramfs locks the kernel down (integrity) before anything else runs: unsigned modules (all modules are signed when the kernel is built, with a key made for that build), unsigned kernels (kexec) and writing to kernel memory are refused. A layer that fails its check, or a missing signed list, stops the start-up with a restart instead of a shell. rudolfd ignores the desktop page on RUDOLFDATA (os/current), which nothing checks.

docs.h: Secure Boot › The chain
docs.t: The boot menu's options are not taken from the menu (the stub ignores them under Secure Boot); the initramfs reads which entry was chosen from the firmware variable LoaderEntrySelected and adds the matching option (rudolf.recovery=1, rudolf.check=1, rudolf.toram=1; rudolf.debug=1 only with Secure Boot off). With Secure Boot off everything works as before, and the layers are still checked: a damaged one is caught, but an unchecked one may start (Task Manager > System says so). BIOS computers start as before (Rudolf Boot). 32-bit UEFI computers are not supported with Secure Boot on.

docs.h: Secure Boot › Keys
docs.t: Rudolf OS Secure Boot key (RSA-2048): made by iso/systools/mksbkey.sh on the maintainer's computer. iso/boot/sb/rudolf-sb.crt. The release build checks that they match (systools/sbkeycheck.py). If the key is ever replaced, every computer must enroll the new certificate (MokManager) before it starts with Secure Boot on. keys in iso/trusted-keys.txt.

docs.h: Secure Boot › Keeping shim current
docs.t: The parts a disc ships are pinned in iso/boot/sb/parts.txt and kept in the draft release sb-parts by the workflow *Secure Boot parts*. Microsoft revokes old shims from time to time (SBAT and the firmware's revocation list); a disc with a revoked shim no longer starts with Secure Boot on. Then: run *Secure Boot parts*, check the new versions in sb-parts.txt of that release, put the new hashes in parts.txt, and make a new disc. Rudolf OS's own SBAT line (rudolf,1, in systools/mkuki.py) is raised if a Rudolf OS kernel bundle must be withdrawn.

docs.h: System reports
docs.t: How a problem reported from Rudolf OS reaches this repository, and how to work with it.

docs.h: System reports › The path of a report
docs.t: 1. On the computer. The person chooses *Report a problem*: Task Manager (bottom right), or Start › Report a problem. They give it a title and say what happened; *Include the system report* is on by default.

docs.h: System reports › The path of a report
docs.t: 2. The system report (sysReport() in desktop/tm26.js) describes the computer at that moment: - Status: Rudolf OS version and installed release, when the report was made, how the computer started (BIOS or UEFI; disc, USB drive or hard disk; live or installed; recovery), whether the desktop runs in the shell or in the plain page (and whether the shell failed), the display mode and size, uptime and load, CPU use, memory and swap, temperature, battery, free storage, network connected or not, the services, open windows and real tabs, and the number of kernel warnings. - Computer: machine and firmware, processor, graphics card and driver, sound cards, storage, network adapters (kind, state, speed), input devices. - Kernel: version, start-up options, drivers, memory in detail. - Processes: the ten using the most memory, the busiest, and the memory of each page (desktop, tabs). - Latest: kernel warnings and errors, the session log, the shell's notes, the desktop's errors.

docs.h: System reports › The path of a report
docs.t: It leaves out what identifies the person: account names, file names, web addresses, network (IP) and hardware (MAC) addresses, e-mail addresses and Wi-Fi network names. The person can read it before sending (*See the report*), save it to C:\DOCUMENTS instead, or leave it out.

docs.h: System reports › The path of a report
docs.t: 3. GitHub. *Continue on GitHub* opens a new issue in Oracle (real tabs keep the GitHub sign-in) with the form .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/system-report.yml filled in through the address: title, *What happened*, version, *Status at the time* and *Full system report*. GitHub refuses very long addresses, so when the full report does not fit, Rudolf OS puts it on the clipboard and the form says to paste it. The person reviews and submits; nothing is sent before that. A GitHub account is needed. Without internet, the dialog says to save the report and send it later.

docs.h: System reports › The path of a report
docs.t: 4. The database. The workflow .github/workflows/system-reports.yml (script .github/scripts/system-reports.js) runs for every issue labelled system-report when it is opened, edited, closed or reopened, and files it in the system-reports branch: - reports/<issue>.json: the record: number, title, link, author, dates, state, version, the problem, every status line (status), and the full report text; - index.json: one line per report, newest first (state, date, version, how it started, desktop, display, memory, warnings, labels), for tools and scripts; - README.md: open reports by version and by area, and a table of all reports, to read on GitHub.

docs.h: System reports › The path of a report
docs.t: It adds labels (version: 1.2.0, area: sound, area: shell when the shell failed, needs: system report when the status is missing) and, for a new issue, a comment with the key status lines.

docs.h: System reports › Working with reports
docs.t: See them: the issues labelled system-report, or the system-reports branch's README for the overview. Filter by version: … and area: … labels. Address one: reply on the issue, fix the area labels if the guess was wrong, link the fix (Fixes #N in the pull request), and close it when the fix is released. Closing updates its state in the database. Missing status: the comment asks the person to paste *Task Manager › Copy system report*; editing the issue files the new text. Look across reports: index.json has every report in one file, for example curl -s https://raw.githubusercontent.com/merciless146/RudolfOS/system-reports/index.json | jq '.[] | select(.state=="open") | .desktop' | sort | uniq -c.

docs.h: System reports › Safety
docs.t: The issue text is written by anyone. The workflow only reads it as data: it is parsed, trimmed and escaped (the README cannot gain links or images from it), the labels come from a fixed list, and nothing from it is run. The workflow has only contents: write and issues: write, writes only the system-reports branch, and takes its script from the default branch. Reports are public. The report leaves out personal details, but the person's own text and anything they paste are theirs to check; the form says so.

docs.h: System reports › Changing the report
docs.t: Add a line to key in sysReport() for something every report should show (it lands in *Status at the time* and, as Key: value, in the record's status), or a section below for details. Field ids in the form (what, version, status, report) are what the desktop fills in; keep them when editing the form.

docs.h: Testing rules for Rudolf OS
docs.t: Written on 2026-11-10 (plan 1.5.8, item 5.4), after the Lite desktop engine passed every check and then closed as it started on the first real computer it reached.

docs.h: Testing rules for Rudolf OS › Anything that changes how the computer or the desktop starts
docs.t: This covers the start-up (initramfs/init), rudolf-init, the session, the desktop engine, the shell, the display (Xorg, Xvfb, rudolf-display), system updates and the boot files. 1. The fallback comes first. Before the change itself reaches a computer, there is a way back that needs no working desktop, and it is tested: a failing desktop engine gives way to the standard one (qt/host/deskfall57_t.sh), a system slot that cannot start gives way to the previous one (qt/host/startfall57_t.sh), Recovery mode starts the installed system with safe settings, and Ctrl+Alt+Backspace starts the safe desktop (qt/host/desksafe58_t.sh).

docs.h: Testing rules for Rudolf OS › Anything that changes how the computer or the desktop starts
docs.t: 2. Test it from the system itself, not from the build machine. A program run on the release machine finds that machine's libraries. Run it from the built layer (a chroot of base.sfs, as webkit-check.yml does), so a library it opens while running (dlopen: graphics, sound, plug-ins) and the layer lacks fails the check. ldd does not see those.

docs.h: Testing rules for Rudolf OS › Anything that changes how the computer or the desktop starts
docs.t: 3. Test it on the real graphics path. Xvfb and LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE hide what the GPU path does. Before such a change reaches the test laptop, it runs once on Xorg with a GPU (QEMU with virtio-gpu, or the laptop over the showed "Couldn't open libGLESv2.so.2" at once). logs are kept (var/log/starts, System health › Last starts), so a start that never reaches the desktop can be read at the next one.

docs.h: Testing rules for Rudolf OS › Everything else
docs.t: Host tests (qt/host/*_t.sh) for scripts and C helpers, with the paths they use moved into a temporary folder. Browser tests (qt/shell2/*_t.js) for the desktop, each on its own port. QEMU only where it is needed: installing, Encrypt my data, moving to a disk, updates and rollback, and the final set before a release is promoted. python3 systools/deadcheck.py (in iso/) before every pull request.

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes
docs.t: Each version's first line after "Summary:" is what Settings shows before an update is installed; the list is what "What's new" and the notification after an update show. The newest version comes first.

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: Summary: Blitzen diagnostics, and what the 1.5.6 tests taught (docs/plan-1.5.7.md)

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: Changed: the Event Viewer's events are kept in your account's folder too (.rudolf/events.log, with your files on the disk), so they outlast the desktop's storage; events from before signing in are written once it is open.

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: Changed: Rudolf OS's service log (rudolfd) is kept on the disk for this start and the 3 before it (/persist/var/log/rudolfd.log, .1 to .3), instead of being lost at each restart.

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: New: ask Blitzen why something went wrong. Error notifications, problems in System health and errors in the Event Viewer have a "⚡ Why?" button, and System health has "What's wrong with this computer?". Blitzen first shows what it will read (the matching log lines and parts of Rudolf OS's documents) and you can leave anything out; it then explains what happened, the likely cause with the log line it comes from, and what you can do. It changes nothing and runs nothing, and it all stays on this computer.

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: New: "Draft a report" under Blitzen's explanation opens Report a problem filled in with it and the log lines it read, for you to check and send yourself.

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: New: files that Rudolf OS deletes on its own, not because you deleted them (a file gone from the desktop's view of your folder some other way, or large files cleared from the Trash's store), are kept for 7 days in "Recovered automatically" at the bottom of the Trash, with Restore and Delete now. System health says what went there and why. Files you delete yourself go to the Trash as before.

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: New: Settings › System health › "Run the self-test" checks, without changing anything, that Linux apps and Debian's programs see your folders, Downloads, the camera, the battery limit, the compressed memory, the desktop's reserved memory, the logs and the Wi-Fi, and says what failed (with "⚡ Why?"). It is also the command rudolf-selftest.

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: Changed: a download the browser held back, or one that stopped arriving, is offered again: its notification downloads it again when clicked, and Downloads (in Oracle) has "Download again" beside every failed download.

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: Fixed: unfinished downloads left behind by the browser stayed in the downloads folder for ever (one from November 4 on a test computer). One that has not grown for a day is now removed, and System health says so.

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: Changed: Battery care remembers which limits this battery does not keep (some laptops keep only 60, 80 or 100 %) and marks them in the list ("this battery keeps 80 % instead").

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: Changed: clearer error messages. The ones you could meet ("write failed (drive full?)", "rpk failed", "no DHCP answer on this network" and others) now say what to do, and clicking the notification opens the Help page about it. "Set up Linux first" now points to Terminal, which has had the Linux tab since 1.5.6.

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: New: Task Manager's Apps lists every app and program that runs, also with no window open (Discord in the tray, Steam half-closed, Windows programs in Wine, Linux programs in Debian), with the memory each uses and "End": it is asked to quit, and stopped if it has not after 5 seconds.

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: New: when memory runs out and Rudolf OS closes an app with no window open, a notification says so at once ("Discord was closed to free memory").

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: New: starting a game while little memory is free and apps run in the background asks first: "Discord is running in the background and uses 640 MB. Close it for the game?"

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: New: Settings › System health › Memory: the memory in use, the compressed memory (Automatic, Smaller or Off, applied at the next restart), what was closed to free memory in the last 7 days, and whether apps with no window open may be closed when memory runs out.

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: Fixed: what the desktop gets from the internet at start-up no longer fails once and waits for the next turn when the Wi-Fi has no address yet. The update check runs once the computer is online (and a failed check is tried again in 5 minutes, not an hour); the Library's list is not kept empty after an offline try; downloading Flathub's app list or Blitzen while offline waits for the internet and then starts by itself; and a page Oracle could not open offline opens by itself once online.

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
docs.t: Changed: the self-test also checks what Linux apps and games need: /dev/fd and /dev/stdin, stdout and stderr (Steam's interface), game controllers, the Linux apps (also in the encrypted folder), Debian with Wine, the windows on screen, and that the compressed memory has the size set in Memory.

docs.h: Rudolf OS changes › 1.5.7 (in progress)
